# Kots's 20%+ Electrostimulation Strength Claims Drew Western Interest but Were Not Replicated

**What it is** — American interest in electrostimulation (ES) as a training adjunct was
aroused in 1971, when Kots in Russia reported increases of more than 20% in muscle
strength, speed and power produced by several weeks of "electrotraining." Unable to
produce comparable results, Canadian researchers invited Kots to lecture at Concordia
University in 1977; armed with the detail that Kots used a sinusoidally modulated 2500 Hz
current source applied in a sequence of 10 seconds of contraction followed by 50 seconds of
relaxation, they again tried to duplicate the Russian claims. The authors report that "researchers
continue to disagree on increase in muscle strength" despite this, and separately note that
various track coaches reported success integrating conventional faradic ES into a
carefully periodised training programme (Francis, 1982). (PDF pp. 219-220, printed pp.
208-209, "4.2.1.1 The Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation.")

**Why it works** — The authors give no physiological mechanism for why Kots's specific
protocol (2500 Hz carrier, 10s on/50s off) would or would not replicate; the chapter's
later "Reasons for Conflicting Research" subsection (see
[[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]]) gives the general
methodological reasons ES research disagrees, without resolving the Kots case specifically.

**When to apply** — Inference: treat any single large ES strength-gain percentage (here,
"more than 20%") as a claim tied to one specific, fully-specified protocol (waveform,
frequency, duty cycle) from one lab, not a generic property of "electrostimulation" as a
category; the Canadian replication attempt failed using a different protocol until they
obtained Kots's exact parameters, and even then the authors do not report the Canadian
outcome as a confirmed success.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single historical claim and a single replication attempt,
both from the 1970s, without independent modern confirmation in this text. Do not cite "20%
plus" as an expected or typical ES strength gain; the chapter itself frames Kots's number as
contested rather than settled, and the following subsection lists nine separate
methodological reasons why ES strength research across studies disagrees.

**Example** — Inference: a strength coach considering NMES for a rehabilitating athlete
should ask what specific waveform, frequency and duty cycle any cited study used, since this
entry shows that even a direct attempt to replicate one well-specified protocol required
obtaining that protocol's exact parameters from its originator before a comparable attempt
could be made.

**Related** — [[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]],
[[case-study--reding-electrostimulation-protocol-siff-account]] (a contemporaneous but
differently-designed elite-athlete ES protocol the authors set against the Kots/Canadian
history).

# Nine Reasons Electrostimulation Strength Research Disagrees: A Checklist for Reading It

**What it is** — The authors give nine specific methodological reasons why published
electrostimulation (ES) strength-training studies contradict one another: (1) many studies
measure only isometric or isokinetic strength change and neglect power, speed, muscular
endurance, residual muscle tension, muscle growth and rate of neuromuscular recovery; (2)
much research uses injured or rehabilitating patients, untrained individuals, or trained
subjects of differing backgrounds, and strength gains are proportionately larger early in
training or in untrained subjects, with early gains driven mainly by neuromuscular
adaptation and learning rather than hypertrophy; (3) ES effectiveness depends on current
intensity and individual tolerance of discomfort, and no waveform has been found to be
universally most comfortable, with considerable inter-subject variation (Delitto & Rose,
1986; Mannheimer & Carlsson, 1979; Moreno-Aranda & Seirig, 1981); (4) effects depend on
waveform type and frequency, since slow-twitch and fast-twitch fibres have distinct
recruitment patterns and functional characteristics (Lloyd et al, 1986; Mannheimer &
Carlsson, 1979; Pette & Vrbova, 1985), and higher frequency (especially with a carrier
wave) lowers electrode-skin impedance and raises comfort; (5) electrode type, size, number,
location and gel affect delivered energy, resultant contraction force and comfort, and many
studies omit these details, "so valid comparisons largely are meaningless"; (6) most
studies use commercial stimulators that vary only a few of the many possible stimulation
parameters (frequency, waveform, pulse-width, modulation type, impulse interval, energy
delivered), so no single study has examined the full parameter space, even in the more
extensive review by Lloyd et al (1986); (7) ES effects, like plyometric training, may be
enhanced or diminished by how well it is integrated into an overall strength and
sport-specific programme (e.g. Francis, 1982); (8) many training regimes are deficiently
designed, setting ES intensity at a fixed value (or a fixed percentage of maximal voluntary
isometric/isokinetic contraction) that does not progress as the subject adapts, the same
flaw that limits fixed-load weight training; (9) the design and effects of a stimulator
depend on which physiological model of cellular communication it assumes (the
action-potential model versus subthreshold/bioelectric models), a design choice most
commercial stimulators do not make explicit (see
[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]]). (PDF pp. 220-221, printed pp.
209-210, "4.2.1.2 Reasons for Conflicting Research.")

**Why it works** — The authors' own framing: these are methodological confounds (measurement
scope, subject population, dosing, hardware specification, and underlying physiological
model), not evidence for or against ES itself; a study that controls for none of these nine
factors cannot be meaningfully compared with one that controls for a different subset.

**When to apply** — Use this as a checklist before citing any single ES strength-training
study: what outcome was measured (item 1), who were the subjects (item 2), was the current
intensity and waveform reported and justified (items 3-4, 6), were electrode details given
(item 5), was the training programme context described (item 7), and did the dosing
progress with adaptation (item 8)? A study missing several of these items should be treated
as weak evidence regardless of its stated conclusion.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this checklist evaluates methodological rigor, not
whether ES "works"; a study can satisfy all nine points and still report a negative or null
result, and the authors elsewhere report both positive and negative ES findings that passed
some of these criteria (see
[[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]]). Do not use this list
to dismiss all ES research wholesale; use it to weight individual studies.

**Example** — Inference: a marketing claim citing "a study showing 20% strength gains from
electrostimulation" should be checked against this list: was the outcome purely isometric
(item 1)? Were the subjects untrained or rehabilitating (item 2)? Was the current intensity
fixed for the whole programme (item 8)? Failing several of these checks should lower
confidence in the claim regardless of the headline number.

**Related** — [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]],
[[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]].

# Seventeen Claimed Clinical and Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation, With Their Original Citations

**What it is** — The authors catalog electrostimulation's (ES) reported applications and
effects, each with cited sources: (1) increase in muscle strength, strongest in
incapacitated, unfit or weakest subjects, with ES alone at best matching or trailing
voluntary exercise, though periodised programmes combining ES with training sometimes
increased competitive athletes' strength (Francis, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Matteson,
1984; Reding, 1973); (2) re-education of faulty muscle-action patterns, e.g. chondromalacia
patellae, tennis elbow, "frozen shoulder" (Eriksson, 1981; Godfrey et al, 1979; Johnson et
al, 1977; Nirschl & Sobel, 1981); (3) facilitation of contraction when voluntary contraction
is blocked by disuse, pain or injury, reducing tissue wasting; (4) increased muscular and
systemic endurance from prolonged sub-maximal ES, with low-frequency (under 15 Hz),
24-hour continuous stimulation shown in animal studies to shift fast-twitch fibres toward a
more aerobic, fatigue-resistant profile (Jolesz & Sreter, 1981; Pette, 1984; Pette & Vrbova,
1985; Salmons & Vrbova, 1969; Salmons & Henriksson, 1981); (5) increased speed of
contraction from long-term, higher-frequency (over 40 Hz) ES, improving reaction time and
decreasing time-to-peak-tension of fast-twitch fibres (Fleury & Lagasse, 1979; Salmons &
Vrbova, 1967, 1969); (6) increased local blood supply, with measured increases from about
20% to over 200%, greatest below roughly 30 Hz (Currier et al, 1986; Richardson, 1981;
Wakim et al, 1948; Wakim, 1953); (7) a massage-like pumping action on venous/lymphatic
return; (8) pain relief via TENS, using low-frequency (50-100 Hz) stimulation without
contraction for superficial pain, or short, high-intensity bursts (1-150 Hz) with
contraction for deeper pain; (9) reduction of protective muscle spasm and spasticity; (10)
promotion of relaxation and recuperation, attributed to central endorphin/enkephalin
release, used by Russian athletes for post-training recuperation and to aid sleep onset even
with mild thigh-only stimulation; (11) increased range of movement, used alongside PNF
mobilisation; (12) reduction of non-infectious swelling; (13) halting or slowing mild to
moderate scoliotic curvature with ES applied to specific back muscles (Axelgaard et al,
1983; Friedman et al, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Schultz et al, 1981); (14) preferential
recruitment of the largest-diameter motor axons first, the reverse of natural recruitment
order, making them a supplementary route to axons that are hard to activate under normal
training (Enoka, 1988); (15) an acute strength increase after a single session: Alon (1985),
studying 14 subjects, found one experimental ES session produced a mean 13% increase in
quadriceps strength; (16) improved metabolic economy: Ratov & Kryazhev (1986) found
electrically stimulating the quadriceps during cycling and speed skating reduced oxygen
consumption by 10-17% and extended time-to-fatigue by 15-20%, and treadmill running with ES
reduced oxygen consumption by about 10%, or by about 5% if the stimulated muscles had just
performed the work; (17) increased contractile speed of skeletal muscle via phasic-type ES.
(PDF pp. 221-224, printed pp. 210-213, "4.2.1.3 Clinical Applications of
Electrostimulation.")

**Why it works** — The authors give a distinct proposed mechanism for each effect
(catalogued above per item) rather than one unifying mechanism; several (items 4-5, 14, 17)
are tied to fibre-type recruitment and conversion, while others (6-13) are tied to blood
flow, central neurochemistry, or mechanical pumping action. Inference: no single theory in
this passage ties all seventeen together; the authors' own attempt at unification is the
separate MACS/MICS theory (see
[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]]).

**When to apply** — Use this as a reference catalog when deciding whether ES could serve a
specific, narrow purpose (e.g. swelling reduction, pain relief, post-training recuperation)
distinct from strength development, which the authors treat as ES's weakest and most
contested claimed benefit (see
[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]). Inference: for Athletic
Medicine or Applied Performance settings, items 6-13 (blood flow, pain, spasm, swelling,
recuperation, ROM) map most directly onto standard rehabilitation and recovery use cases,
while items 1-5, 14-17 (strength, endurance, speed, recruitment, metabolic economy) are the
more contested performance-training claims.

**When NOT to apply** — Each item rests on citations from roughly 1948-1988, mostly single
studies or small samples (e.g. Alon's 13% figure is from 14 subjects, one session); none are
independently re-validated within this ingest. Item 4's fibre-type conversion evidence is
from animal (cross-innervation, continuous 24-hour stimulation) studies, not directly
transferable to standard clinical ES dosing. Do not treat this list as equally strong
evidence across all seventeen items; some (blood flow, pain relief, swelling) have broader
citation support here than others (scoliosis, acute strength).

**Example** — Inference: a post-training recovery application (item 10, low-current
stimulation to aid relaxation and sleep onset) is a narrower, better-supported use case than
citing this same list to justify ES as a primary strength-training tool (item 1, contested
above); a practitioner should not conflate the two when deciding whether to add ES to a
program.

[[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]],
[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]].

# The Authors' MACS/MICS Theory of Electrostimulation: A Speculative Synthesis, Not a Settled Mechanism

**What it is** — Building on research showing that very low currents (as little as 10
microamps, far below the milliamp-range currents of standard faradic/TENS devices) can
match or exceed conventional electrostimulation's (ES) benefits without causing contraction,
pain blockade or heating (Matteson & Eberhardt, 1985), the authors propose an "integrated
theory": macroelectric cellular stimulation (**MACS**, currents exceeding one milliamp) acts
as a physiological stressor producing Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome-type alarm
response (citing Eriksson et al, 1981, who found traditional ES's acute effects resemble
intense voluntary exercise; and Gambke et al, 1985, who found in animal studies that
long-term MACS causes some, mainly fast-twitch, fibres to degenerate and be replaced via
satellite-cell proliferation). Applying Selye's model (see 1.16), the body would draw on
"superficial adaptation energy stores" to adapt to MACS via increased strength, endurance,
or fibre-type transformation; if the ES is too intense, prolonged or misapplied, adaptation
might fail or shift toward slow-twitch fibres and reduced strength, and "excessively
demanding MACS conceivably might cause the body to draw on its deep adaptation energy and
lead to permanent tissue damage." Microelectric cellular stimulation (**MICS**, currents
below one milliamp) is proposed not to act as a stressor at all, but to elicit biochemical
changes tied to "resonant attunement" of the stimulus to cellular/subcellular processes,
citing a chain of supporting findings: Becker and colleagues on sub-threshold modulation of
electric fields across nerve and glial cells regulating growth and communication, including
wound-healing acceleration and partial limb regeneration in animals (Becker, 1974; Becker &
Marino, 1982); Nordenstrom's proposed "closed electric circuits" in the body carrying ionic
flow via blood vessels (Nordenstrom, 1983); Pilla's (1974) electrochemical membrane-signaling
model and "cellular windows" that respond most to specific frequencies, pulse widths and
amplitudes (Pilla, 1981); Rodan et al (1978), who found 5 Hz ES stimulated DNA synthesis in
chick cartilage and rat bone by up to 27% (but not in chick skin fibroblasts or rat spleen
lymphocytes) 4-6 hours after 15 minutes of stimulation; and Cheng et al (1982), who found
50-1000 microamp currents increased rat tissue ATP concentration by 300-500% and amino-acid
transport/protein synthesis by up to 40%, while currents above one milliamp depressed ATP
and protein synthesis (traditional ES commonly exceeds 20 milliamps, at which point this
depression is "nearly 50%"). Practical implication drawn from the theory: MICS can be used
far more routinely than MACS, since it "cannot produce overtraining or injury," while MACS
should be dosed and progressed like any other training stressor. (PDF pp. 224-227, printed
pp. 213-216, "4.2.1.4 Further Research Findings" and "4.2.1.5 An Integrated Theory of
Electrostimulation.")

**Why it works** — This is the authors' own proposed synthesis, not a mechanism independently
established elsewhere in the text. It rests on two distinct evidentiary threads of very
different standing: (a) a defensible, mainstream physiological point that MACS-range ES acts
as a training/adaptation stressor subject to a dose-response and overtraining risk (the
Selye/Eriksson/Gambke citations); and (b) a set of bioelectromagnetic claims (Becker's
regeneration work, Nordenstrom's "biologically closed electric circuits," Pilla's cellular
windows) that were speculative even by 1990s standards and have not entered mainstream
sports-science or clinical practice as the general theory of cell communication the authors
present them as. The authors themselves flag some of this as still-developing: "little is
known about electrical fields at the subcellular level," and classical action-potential
theory "does not explain the mechanisms whereby electric and other fields stimulate
processes such as the repair of fractures... and reduction of thrombosis" (printed 210).

**When to apply** — Inference: the (a) thread, that macro-current ES functions as a
stressor requiring progressive dosing rather than a fixed protocol, is a reasonable,
generally-applicable caution consistent with basic training-load principles and does not
depend on accepting thread (b). Do not use this entry to justify low-current "microcurrent"
devices for performance claims (tissue repair beyond standard wound-healing use, cellular
"resonance," or Nordenstrom-style circuit theory) without independent, modern verification
outside this book.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked contested: several supporting claims in thread (b) (glial-cell
signaling as a major regulatory pathway comparable to semiconductor circuits; Nordenstrom's
"closed electric circuits"; "resonant attunement" as the operative principle of MICS) are
not mainstream, independently-replicated physiology as of this ingest, and this entry does
not attempt to verify them against current literature. The Rodan (1978) and Cheng (1982)
findings are animal/cell-culture studies (chick cartilage, rat bone, rat tissue) at specific
narrow current ranges; they do not establish that MICS produces the general "growth,
adaptation and repair" effects the authors attribute to it in human athletes. Do not treat
"MACS" and "MICS" as terms used outside this text; they appear to be the authors' own
coinage for this section.

**Example** — Inference: a practitioner who reads "10-microamp microcurrent devices are as
effective as faradic stimulators without the risks" should recognize this claim rests
primarily on thread (b) above (Becker, Nordenstrom, Pilla), not on independently replicated
modern evidence, and should treat performance or healing claims for such devices with the
same skepticism the authors themselves apply to unverified action-potential-only models.

**Related** — [[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]],
[[heuristic--electrostimulation-sequencing-dosage-and-safety-practicalities]] (the
practical dosing limits the authors draw partly from this theory).

# Ratov's Functional Electrostimulation (FES): Timing the Current to the Athlete's Own EMG Signal During the Sport Skill Itself

**What it is** — Siff writes in the first person that "little or no mention is made in the
West" of Functional Electrostimulation (FES, called FENS in the West), which in the West
refers narrowly to using ES to produce movement in spinally disabled patients who cannot
voluntarily activate their muscles. In Russia and other Eastern European countries the term
also covers a different application: applying electrostimulation to able-bodied athletes
during natural sporting movements, timed to intensify muscle tension at the most
appropriate phase of the movement itself. Professor Igor Ratov of the State Central
Institute of Sports Science in Moscow developed this from his PhD work on the interrelation
between electrical stimulation and electromyography, using EMG signals from agonist and
antagonist muscles as triggers or control mechanisms to phase electrical stimulation into
the specific phases of a functional sporting movement. Ratov applied this with fencers,
boxers, rowers, shotputters and weightlifters, and, per Siff's first-person account of
witnessing the work in Ratov's laboratory, used concurrent EMG recordings "to phase the FES
correctly into specific sporting movements, most specifically to avoid producing spurious
muscle tension or uncoordinated movement." Over time, athletes learn to contract their
muscles synchronously with the externally applied electrical field, said to produce greater
strength, power and speed; this is called "active electrostimulation" (applied to actively
contracting muscles) as distinct from "passive electrostimulation" (applied to relaxed
muscles), the latter being the method most common in physical therapy. Ratov reportedly
"stresses that this type of functional stimulation is far more consistently successful than
the passive methods attributed to Kots by his Western supporters" (see
[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]). (PDF pp. 226-227, printed
pp. 215-216, "4.2.1.6 The Use of Electrostimulation in Training," "Sports Functional
Electrostimulation.")

**Why it works** — The stated logic: because the electrical stimulus is phased by the
athlete's own real-time EMG signal into the correct part of the movement (rather than
applied on a fixed, movement-independent schedule as in passive/general ES), it can
intensify muscle tension precisely when and where the sport skill needs it without disrupting
the coordinated movement pattern. Inference: no data (strength gain percentages, EMG
amplitude changes, performance-test results) are reported for this method in this passage;
the claim of superiority over passive ES is Ratov's own stated position, as reported by
Siff, not a cited experimental comparison.

**When to apply** — Inference: relevant to anyone considering EMG-triggered or
movement-phased electrical stimulation for sport-specific training (as opposed to general
or isolated-muscle ES); the distinguishing feature to look for in any modern device or
protocol claiming this lineage is real-time EMG-based triggering synchronized to the
athlete's own voluntary movement, not a fixed timing schedule.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: no quantitative outcome data are reported for Ratov's
method in this passage, only a description of the approach and Siff's first-hand
observation that it was applied with named elite-sport categories (fencers, boxers, rowers,
shotputters, weightlifters). The claimed superiority over passive ES ("far more consistently
successful") is reported as Ratov's own assessment via Siff, not verified against a cited
trial. Access to this specific method also depended on specialized laboratory equipment (EMG-linked
stimulators) not generally available.

**Example** — The book's own example is Ratov's application with the named sport
categories above (fencers, boxers, rowers, shotputters, weightlifters), reported by Siff as
directly observed; no further invented example is added here.

[[case-study--reding-electrostimulation-protocol-siff-account]].

15	# Case Study: Siff's First-Hand Account of Serge Reding's Electrostimulation Protocol
16	
17	**What it is** — This passage is Siff writing in the first person about his own direct
18	training contact with Serge Reding, a Belgian superheavyweight weightlifter, "who had close
19	training contact with one of the authors (Siff) while he stayed with him in South Africa in
20	the early 1970s" (citing Siff, 1973). Reding's post-session electrostimulation (ES) protocol
21	differed from Kots's (see
22	[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]): 0.5 to 2 second, very
23	high intensity contractions with 10 to 15 second rest periods, for a total of 5 minutes per
24	major muscle group, with agonists and antagonists of each limb alternately stimulated in
25	ipsilateral and contralateral sequences. Reding always concluded sessions with a few
26	repetitions (1-3) of a long-duration (10-15 second), fairly intense tetanic contraction
27	used as a form of deep massage, followed by about 10-15 minutes of microcurrent stimulation
28	(less than 200 microamps) applied across the head and spinal cord with a separate
29	electrostimulator. Elsewhere in the section, Siff again writes in the first person: "the ES
30	training applied to the author by Serge Reding used a Myogen Parametric stimulator that was
31	designed to offer external stimulation which in no way simulated the most frequently
32	occurring movements of Olympic lifting," used as a form of General Physical Preparation
33	(GPP) rather than sport-specific stimulation; Reding stressed the importance of different
34	waveforms and regimes for different sport categories, "adding that the method shared by
35	Kots with Canadian coaches was only one of many possibilities." (PDF p. 220, printed p.
36	209; PDF p. 226, printed p. 215, "4.2.1.1" and "4.2.1.6 The Use of Electrostimulation in
37	Training.")
38	
39	**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why this specific dosing pattern (brief,
40	high-intensity contractions; alternating ipsilateral/contralateral agonist-antagonist
41	sequencing; a closing deep-massage-style tetanic contraction; low-current cranial-spinal
42	microstimulation) would produce a training effect; the passage is a descriptive account of
43	practice, not an experiment.
44	
45	**When to apply** — Inference: use this as a documented example that elite-level ES
46	protocols in this era varied substantially even among people working with the same broad
47	technology (faradic/interferential ES devices); it is not evidence that Reding's specific
48	protocol outperformed Kots's, only that it existed and was applied to a top-level athlete
49	under Siff's direct observation.
50	
51	**When NOT to apply** — Untested: this is a single first-person account (n = 1, Siff
52	observing/administering) with no reported outcome data (no before/after strength numbers),
53	no control condition, and no independent replication in the text. Do not treat the specific
54	timings (0.5-2s contractions, 10-15s rest, 5 min per muscle group, 10-15 min microcurrent
55	under 200 microamps) as a validated prescription; they are a description of what one
56	coach-athlete pair did.
57	
58	**Example** — The book's own example is this case itself: Reding's own protocol as directly
59	witnessed and partly administered by Siff. No further invented example is added here.

78	# Kots's 20%+ Electrostimulation Strength Claims Drew Western Interest but Were Not Replicated
79	
80	**What it is** — American interest in electrostimulation (ES) as a training adjunct was
81	aroused in 1971, when Kots in Russia reported increases of more than 20% in muscle
82	strength, speed and power produced by several weeks of "electrotraining." Unable to
83	produce comparable results, Canadian researchers invited Kots to lecture at Concordia
84	University in 1977; armed with the detail that Kots used a sinusoidally modulated 2500 Hz
85	current source applied in a sequence of 10 seconds of contraction followed by 50 seconds of
86	relaxation, they again tried to duplicate the Russian claims. The authors report that "researchers
87	continue to disagree on increase in muscle strength" despite this, and separately note that
88	various track coaches reported success integrating conventional faradic ES into a
89	carefully periodised training programme (Francis, 1982). (PDF pp. 219-220, printed pp.
90	208-209, "4.2.1.1 The Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation.")
91	
92	**Why it works** — The authors give no physiological mechanism for why Kots's specific
93	protocol (2500 Hz carrier, 10s on/50s off) would or would not replicate; the chapter's
94	later "Reasons for Conflicting Research" subsection (see
95	[[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]]) gives the general
96	methodological reasons ES research disagrees, without resolving the Kots case specifically.
97	
98	**When to apply** — Inference: treat any single large ES strength-gain percentage (here,
99	"more than 20%") as a claim tied to one specific, fully-specified protocol (waveform,
100	frequency, duty cycle) from one lab, not a generic property of "electrostimulation" as a
101	category; the Canadian replication attempt failed using a different protocol until they
102	obtained Kots's exact parameters, and even then the authors do not report the Canadian
103	outcome as a confirmed success.
104	
105	**When NOT to apply** — This is a single historical claim and a single replication attempt,
106	both from the 1970s, without independent modern confirmation in this text. Do not cite "20%
107	plus" as an expected or typical ES strength gain; the chapter itself frames Kots's number as
108	contested rather than settled, and the following subsection lists nine separate
109	methodological reasons why ES strength research across studies disagrees.
110	
111	**Example** — Inference: a strength coach considering NMES for a rehabilitating athlete
112	should ask what specific waveform, frequency and duty cycle any cited study used, since this
113	entry shows that even a direct attempt to replicate one well-specified protocol required
114	obtaining that protocol's exact parameters from its originator before a comparable attempt
115	could be made.
116

118	[[case-study--reding-electrostimulation-protocol-siff-account]] (a contemporaneous but
119	differently-designed elite-athlete ES protocol the authors set against the Kots/Canadian
120	history).

134	
135	# Nine Reasons Electrostimulation Strength Research Disagrees: A Checklist for Reading It
136	
137	**What it is** — The authors give nine specific methodological reasons why published
138	electrostimulation (ES) strength-training studies contradict one another: (1) many studies
139	measure only isometric or isokinetic strength change and neglect power, speed, muscular
140	endurance, residual muscle tension, muscle growth and rate of neuromuscular recovery; (2)
141	much research uses injured or rehabilitating patients, untrained individuals, or trained
142	subjects of differing backgrounds, and strength gains are proportionately larger early in
143	training or in untrained subjects, with early gains driven mainly by neuromuscular
144	adaptation and learning rather than hypertrophy; (3) ES effectiveness depends on current
145	intensity and individual tolerance of discomfort, and no waveform has been found to be
146	universally most comfortable, with considerable inter-subject variation (Delitto & Rose,
147	1986; Mannheimer & Carlsson, 1979; Moreno-Aranda & Seirig, 1981); (4) effects depend on
148	waveform type and frequency, since slow-twitch and fast-twitch fibres have distinct
149	recruitment patterns and functional characteristics (Lloyd et al, 1986; Mannheimer &
150	Carlsson, 1979; Pette & Vrbova, 1985), and higher frequency (especially with a carrier
151	wave) lowers electrode-skin impedance and raises comfort; (5) electrode type, size, number,
152	location and gel affect delivered energy, resultant contraction force and comfort, and many
153	studies omit these details, "so valid comparisons largely are meaningless"; (6) most
154	studies use commercial stimulators that vary only a few of the many possible stimulation
155	parameters (frequency, waveform, pulse-width, modulation type, impulse interval, energy
156	delivered), so no single study has examined the full parameter space, even in the more
157	extensive review by Lloyd et al (1986); (7) ES effects, like plyometric training, may be
158	enhanced or diminished by how well it is integrated into an overall strength and
159	sport-specific programme (e.g. Francis, 1982); (8) many training regimes are deficiently
160	designed, setting ES intensity at a fixed value (or a fixed percentage of maximal voluntary
161	isometric/isokinetic contraction) that does not progress as the subject adapts, the same
162	flaw that limits fixed-load weight training; (9) the design and effects of a stimulator
163	depend on which physiological model of cellular communication it assumes (the
164	action-potential model versus subthreshold/bioelectric models), a design choice most
165	commercial stimulators do not make explicit (see
166	[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]]). (PDF pp. 220-221, printed pp.
167	209-210, "4.2.1.2 Reasons for Conflicting Research.")
168	
169	**Why it works** — The authors' own framing: these are methodological confounds (measurement
170	scope, subject population, dosing, hardware specification, and underlying physiological
171	model), not evidence for or against ES itself; a study that controls for none of these nine
172	factors cannot be meaningfully compared with one that controls for a different subset.
173	
174	**When to apply** — Use this as a checklist before citing any single ES strength-training
175	study: what outcome was measured (item 1), who were the subjects (item 2), was the current
176	intensity and waveform reported and justified (items 3-4, 6), were electrode details given
177	(item 5), was the training programme context described (item 7), and did the dosing
178	progress with adaptation (item 8)? A study missing several of these items should be treated
179	as weak evidence regardless of its stated conclusion.
180	
181	**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this checklist evaluates methodological rigor, not
182	whether ES "works"; a study can satisfy all nine points and still report a negative or null
183	result, and the authors elsewhere report both positive and negative ES findings that passed
184	some of these criteria (see
185	[[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]]). Do not use this list
186	to dismiss all ES research wholesale; use it to weight individual studies.
187	
188	**Example** — Inference: a marketing claim citing "a study showing 20% strength gains from
189	electrostimulation" should be checked against this list: was the outcome purely isometric
190	(item 1)? Were the subjects untrained or rehabilitating (item 2)? Was the current intensity
191	fixed for the whole programme (item 8)? Failing several of these checks should lower
192	confidence in the claim regardless of the headline number.
193	
194	**Related** — [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]],
195	[[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]].

210	# Seventeen Claimed Clinical and Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation, With Their Original Citations
211	
212	**What it is** — The authors catalog electrostimulation's (ES) reported applications and
213	effects, each with cited sources: (1) increase in muscle strength, strongest in
214	incapacitated, unfit or weakest subjects, with ES alone at best matching or trailing
215	voluntary exercise, though periodised programmes combining ES with training sometimes
216	increased competitive athletes' strength (Francis, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Matteson,
217	1984; Reding, 1973); (2) re-education of faulty muscle-action patterns, e.g. chondromalacia
218	patellae, tennis elbow, "frozen shoulder" (Eriksson, 1981; Godfrey et al, 1979; Johnson et
219	al, 1977; Nirschl & Sobel, 1981); (3) facilitation of contraction when voluntary contraction
220	is blocked by disuse, pain or injury, reducing tissue wasting; (4) increased muscular and
221	systemic endurance from prolonged sub-maximal ES, with low-frequency (under 15 Hz),
222	24-hour continuous stimulation shown in animal studies to shift fast-twitch fibres toward a
223	more aerobic, fatigue-resistant profile (Jolesz & Sreter, 1981; Pette, 1984; Pette & Vrbova,
224	1985; Salmons & Vrbova, 1969; Salmons & Henriksson, 1981); (5) increased speed of
225	contraction from long-term, higher-frequency (over 40 Hz) ES, improving reaction time and
226	decreasing time-to-peak-tension of fast-twitch fibres (Fleury & Lagasse, 1979; Salmons &
227	Vrbova, 1967, 1969); (6) increased local blood supply, with measured increases from about
228	20% to over 200%, greatest below roughly 30 Hz (Currier et al, 1986; Richardson, 1981;
229	Wakim et al, 1948; Wakim, 1953); (7) a massage-like pumping action on venous/lymphatic
230	return; (8) pain relief via TENS, using low-frequency (50-100 Hz) stimulation without
231	contraction for superficial pain, or short, high-intensity bursts (1-150 Hz) with
232	contraction for deeper pain; (9) reduction of protective muscle spasm and spasticity; (10)
233	promotion of relaxation and recuperation, attributed to central endorphin/enkephalin
234	release, used by Russian athletes for post-training recuperation and to aid sleep onset even
235	with mild thigh-only stimulation; (11) increased range of movement, used alongside PNF
236	mobilisation; (12) reduction of non-infectious swelling; (13) halting or slowing mild to
237	moderate scoliotic curvature with ES applied to specific back muscles (Axelgaard et al,
238	1983; Friedman et al, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Schultz et al, 1981); (14) preferential
239	recruitment of the largest-diameter motor axons first, the reverse of natural recruitment
240	order, making them a supplementary route to axons that are hard to activate under normal
241	training (Enoka, 1988); (15) an acute strength increase after a single session: Alon (1985),
242	studying 14 subjects, found one experimental ES session produced a mean 13% increase in
243	quadriceps strength; (16) improved metabolic economy: Ratov & Kryazhev (1986) found
244	electrically stimulating the quadriceps during cycling and speed skating reduced oxygen
245	consumption by 10-17% and extended time-to-fatigue by 15-20%, and treadmill running with ES
246	reduced oxygen consumption by about 10%, or by about 5% if the stimulated muscles had just
247	performed the work; (17) increased contractile speed of skeletal muscle via phasic-type ES.
248	(PDF pp. 221-224, printed pp. 210-213, "4.2.1.3 Clinical Applications of
249	Electrostimulation.")
250	
251	**Why it works** — The authors give a distinct proposed mechanism for each effect
252	(catalogued above per item) rather than one unifying mechanism; several (items 4-5, 14, 17)
253	are tied to fibre-type recruitment and conversion, while others (6-13) are tied to blood
254	flow, central neurochemistry, or mechanical pumping action. Inference: no single theory in
255	this passage ties all seventeen together; the authors' own attempt at unification is the
256	separate MACS/MICS theory (see
257	[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]]).
258	
259	**When to apply** — Use this as a reference catalog when deciding whether ES could serve a
260	specific, narrow purpose (e.g. swelling reduction, pain relief, post-training recuperation)
261	distinct from strength development, which the authors treat as ES's weakest and most
262	contested claimed benefit (see
263	[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]). Inference: for Athletic
264	Medicine or Applied Performance settings, items 6-13 (blood flow, pain, spasm, swelling,
265	recuperation, ROM) map most directly onto standard rehabilitation and recovery use cases,
266	while items 1-5, 14-17 (strength, endurance, speed, recruitment, metabolic economy) are the
267	more contested performance-training claims.
268	
269	**When NOT to apply** — Each item rests on citations from roughly 1948-1988, mostly single
270	studies or small samples (e.g. Alon's 13% figure is from 14 subjects, one session); none are
271	independently re-validated within this ingest. Item 4's fibre-type conversion evidence is
272	from animal (cross-innervation, continuous 24-hour stimulation) studies, not directly
273	transferable to standard clinical ES dosing. Do not treat this list as equally strong
274	evidence across all seventeen items; some (blood flow, pain relief, swelling) have broader
275	citation support here than others (scoliosis, acute strength).
276	
277	**Example** — Inference: a post-training recovery application (item 10, low-current
278	stimulation to aid relaxation and sleep onset) is a narrower, better-supported use case than
279	citing this same list to justify ES as a primary strength-training tool (item 1, contested
280	above); a practitioner should not conflate the two when deciding whether to add ES to a
281	program.
282

300	# The Authors' MACS/MICS Theory of Electrostimulation: A Speculative Synthesis, Not a Settled Mechanism
301	
302	**What it is** — Building on research showing that very low currents (as little as 10
303	microamps, far below the milliamp-range currents of standard faradic/TENS devices) can
304	match or exceed conventional electrostimulation's (ES) benefits without causing contraction,
305	pain blockade or heating (Matteson & Eberhardt, 1985), the authors propose an "integrated
306	theory": macroelectric cellular stimulation (**MACS**, currents exceeding one milliamp) acts
307	as a physiological stressor producing Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome-type alarm
308	response (citing Eriksson et al, 1981, who found traditional ES's acute effects resemble
309	intense voluntary exercise; and Gambke et al, 1985, who found in animal studies that
310	long-term MACS causes some, mainly fast-twitch, fibres to degenerate and be replaced via
311	satellite-cell proliferation). Applying Selye's model (see 1.16), the body would draw on
312	"superficial adaptation energy stores" to adapt to MACS via increased strength, endurance,
313	or fibre-type transformation; if the ES is too intense, prolonged or misapplied, adaptation
314	might fail or shift toward slow-twitch fibres and reduced strength, and "excessively
315	demanding MACS conceivably might cause the body to draw on its deep adaptation energy and
316	lead to permanent tissue damage." Microelectric cellular stimulation (**MICS**, currents
317	below one milliamp) is proposed not to act as a stressor at all, but to elicit biochemical
318	changes tied to "resonant attunement" of the stimulus to cellular/subcellular processes,
319	citing a chain of supporting findings: Becker and colleagues on sub-threshold modulation of
320	electric fields across nerve and glial cells regulating growth and communication, including
321	wound-healing acceleration and partial limb regeneration in animals (Becker, 1974; Becker &
322	Marino, 1982); Nordenstrom's proposed "closed electric circuits" in the body carrying ionic
323	flow via blood vessels (Nordenstrom, 1983); Pilla's (1974) electrochemical membrane-signaling
324	model and "cellular windows" that respond most to specific frequencies, pulse widths and
325	amplitudes (Pilla, 1981); Rodan et al (1978), who found 5 Hz ES stimulated DNA synthesis in
326	chick cartilage and rat bone by up to 27% (but not in chick skin fibroblasts or rat spleen
327	lymphocytes) 4-6 hours after 15 minutes of stimulation; and Cheng et al (1982), who found
328	50-1000 microamp currents increased rat tissue ATP concentration by 300-500% and amino-acid
329	transport/protein synthesis by up to 40%, while currents above one milliamp depressed ATP
330	and protein synthesis (traditional ES commonly exceeds 20 milliamps, at which point this
331	depression is "nearly 50%"). Practical implication drawn from the theory: MICS can be used
332	far more routinely than MACS, since it "cannot produce overtraining or injury," while MACS
333	should be dosed and progressed like any other training stressor. (PDF pp. 224-227, printed
334	pp. 213-216, "4.2.1.4 Further Research Findings" and "4.2.1.5 An Integrated Theory of
335	Electrostimulation.")
336	
337	**Why it works** — This is the authors' own proposed synthesis, not a mechanism independently
338	established elsewhere in the text. It rests on two distinct evidentiary threads of very
339	different standing: (a) a defensible, mainstream physiological point that MACS-range ES acts
340	as a training/adaptation stressor subject to a dose-response and overtraining risk (the
341	Selye/Eriksson/Gambke citations); and (b) a set of bioelectromagnetic claims (Becker's
342	regeneration work, Nordenstrom's "biologically closed electric circuits," Pilla's cellular
343	windows) that were speculative even by 1990s standards and have not entered mainstream
344	sports-science or clinical practice as the general theory of cell communication the authors
345	present them as. The authors themselves flag some of this as still-developing: "little is
346	known about electrical fields at the subcellular level," and classical action-potential
347	theory "does not explain the mechanisms whereby electric and other fields stimulate
348	processes such as the repair of fractures... and reduction of thrombosis" (printed 210).
349	
350	**When to apply** — Inference: the (a) thread, that macro-current ES functions as a
351	stressor requiring progressive dosing rather than a fixed protocol, is a reasonable,
352	generally-applicable caution consistent with basic training-load principles and does not
353	depend on accepting thread (b). Do not use this entry to justify low-current "microcurrent"
354	devices for performance claims (tissue repair beyond standard wound-healing use, cellular
355	"resonance," or Nordenstrom-style circuit theory) without independent, modern verification
356	outside this book.
357	
358	**When NOT to apply** — Marked contested: several supporting claims in thread (b) (glial-cell
359	signaling as a major regulatory pathway comparable to semiconductor circuits; Nordenstrom's
360	"closed electric circuits"; "resonant attunement" as the operative principle of MICS) are
361	not mainstream, independently-replicated physiology as of this ingest, and this entry does
362	not attempt to verify them against current literature. The Rodan (1978) and Cheng (1982)
363	findings are animal/cell-culture studies (chick cartilage, rat bone, rat tissue) at specific
364	narrow current ranges; they do not establish that MICS produces the general "growth,
365	adaptation and repair" effects the authors attribute to it in human athletes. Do not treat
366	"MACS" and "MICS" as terms used outside this text; they appear to be the authors' own
367	coinage for this section.
368	
369	**Example** — Inference: a practitioner who reads "10-microamp microcurrent devices are as
370	effective as faradic stimulators without the risks" should recognize this claim rests
371	primarily on thread (b) above (Becker, Nordenstrom, Pilla), not on independently replicated
372	modern evidence, and should treat performance or healing claims for such devices with the
373	same skepticism the authors themselves apply to unverified action-potential-only models.
374	
375	**Related** — [[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]],
376	[[heuristic--electrostimulation-sequencing-dosage-and-safety-practicalities]] (the
377	practical dosing limits the authors draw partly from this theory).

392	# Ratov's Functional Electrostimulation (FES): Timing the Current to the Athlete's Own EMG Signal During the Sport Skill Itself
393	
394	**What it is** — Siff writes in the first person that "little or no mention is made in the
395	West" of Functional Electrostimulation (FES, called FENS in the West), which in the West
396	refers narrowly to using ES to produce movement in spinally disabled patients who cannot
397	voluntarily activate their muscles. In Russia and other Eastern European countries the term
398	also covers a different application: applying electrostimulation to able-bodied athletes
399	during natural sporting movements, timed to intensify muscle tension at the most
400	appropriate phase of the movement itself. Professor Igor Ratov of the State Central
401	Institute of Sports Science in Moscow developed this from his PhD work on the interrelation
402	between electrical stimulation and electromyography, using EMG signals from agonist and
403	antagonist muscles as triggers or control mechanisms to phase electrical stimulation into
404	the specific phases of a functional sporting movement. Ratov applied this with fencers,
405	boxers, rowers, shotputters and weightlifters, and, per Siff's first-person account of
406	witnessing the work in Ratov's laboratory, used concurrent EMG recordings "to phase the FES
407	correctly into specific sporting movements, most specifically to avoid producing spurious
408	muscle tension or uncoordinated movement." Over time, athletes learn to contract their
409	muscles synchronously with the externally applied electrical field, said to produce greater
410	strength, power and speed; this is called "active electrostimulation" (applied to actively
411	contracting muscles) as distinct from "passive electrostimulation" (applied to relaxed
412	muscles), the latter being the method most common in physical therapy. Ratov reportedly
413	"stresses that this type of functional stimulation is far more consistently successful than
414	the passive methods attributed to Kots by his Western supporters" (see
415	[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]). (PDF pp. 226-227, printed
416	pp. 215-216, "4.2.1.6 The Use of Electrostimulation in Training," "Sports Functional
417	Electrostimulation.")
418	
419	**Why it works** — The stated logic: because the electrical stimulus is phased by the
420	athlete's own real-time EMG signal into the correct part of the movement (rather than
421	applied on a fixed, movement-independent schedule as in passive/general ES), it can
422	intensify muscle tension precisely when and where the sport skill needs it without disrupting
423	the coordinated movement pattern. Inference: no data (strength gain percentages, EMG
424	amplitude changes, performance-test results) are reported for this method in this passage;
425	the claim of superiority over passive ES is Ratov's own stated position, as reported by
426	Siff, not a cited experimental comparison.
427	
428	**When to apply** — Inference: relevant to anyone considering EMG-triggered or
429	movement-phased electrical stimulation for sport-specific training (as opposed to general
430	or isolated-muscle ES); the distinguishing feature to look for in any modern device or
431	protocol claiming this lineage is real-time EMG-based triggering synchronized to the
432	athlete's own voluntary movement, not a fixed timing schedule.
433	
434	**When NOT to apply** — Untested: no quantitative outcome data are reported for Ratov's
435	method in this passage, only a description of the approach and Siff's first-hand
436	observation that it was applied with named elite-sport categories (fencers, boxers, rowers,
437	shotputters, weightlifters). The claimed superiority over passive ES ("far more consistently
438	successful") is reported as Ratov's own assessment via Siff, not verified against a cited
439	trial. Access to this specific method also depended on specialized laboratory equipment (EMG-linked
440	stimulators) not generally available.
441	
442	**Example** — The book's own example is Ratov's application with the named sport
443	categories above (fencers, boxers, rowers, shotputters, weightlifters), reported by Siff as
444	directly observed; no further invented example is added here.
445	
446	**Related** — [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]],
447	[[case-study--reding-electrostimulation-protocol-siff-account]].

462	# Practical Rules for Integrating Electrostimulation Into a Programme: Sequencing, Electrode Placement, Dose Limits
463	
464	**What it is** — Several Russian researchers (Purvin, Deniskin, Khodykin, cited without
465	individual dates) studied how electrostimulation (ES) combines with other training means and
466	found that using ES first, followed by plyometrics, produces a greater training effect than
467	the reverse order; a still larger effect came from using ES and plyometrics concurrently
468	with heavy resistance exercise, while the ES-plyometric combination had its smallest
469	training effect during periods of complete or partial rest. Electrode placement matters:
470	adjacent (close) electrode attachment localises the contraction and keeps it fairly
471	superficial, while distant attachment (one electrode placed at a remote or neutral site)
472	produces a more extensive, deeper contraction; electrode gel or weak saline solution is
473	needed for comfortable conduction, and skin irritation or prickliness "invariably" results
474	from the gel drying out. Placing electrodes directly over major nerves increases contraction
475	intensity but "can be harmful," and the authors restrict this to use by experienced physical
476	therapists. On dosing: it is "generally not advisable to apply more than 5-10 minutes of
477	intense ES per major muscle group," due to associated tissue necrosis and prolonged soreness
478	that can follow (see [[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]] for the
479	macroelectric/microelectric distinction behind this limit); biofeedback TENS devices that
480	monitor cellular electrical characteristics and adjust parameters automatically reduce
481	overstimulation risk. The authors' closing recommendation is that "the untutored reader is
482	not encouraged to use ES," since safe, effective application "requires considerable
483	theoretical and practical training," and that casual users typically see only sporadic,
484	short-term progress before discontinuing within a few months; in several countries
485	(the authors name the USA), ES devices may not legally be sold to the public or used
486	commercially by anyone without medical or physiotherapy training. (PDF pp. 225-227, printed
487	pp. 214-216, "4.2.1.6 The Use of Electrostimulation in Training.")
488	
489	**Why it works** — For the sequencing finding, the authors give no separate mechanism here
490	beyond the general after-effect logic already stated for training order (see
491	[[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]): ES applied first may
492	potentiate the neuromuscular state for the plyometric work that follows, and the combined
493	concurrent condition with heavy resistance stacks all three stimuli within the same session
494	window. For electrode placement, the mechanism is straightforwardly the current's path
495	through tissue between the two electrode sites. For the dose limit, the mechanism given
496	(tissue necrosis, prolonged soreness) implies macro-current ES imposes real mechanical/metabolic
497	stress on the stimulated tissue, consistent with the MACS-as-stressor framing.
498	
499	**When to apply** — Use the sequencing finding (ES before plyometrics beats the reverse; ES
500	plus plyometrics concurrent with heavy resistance beats either combination alone) as a
501	specific instance of the book's broader non-commutative-training-order argument (see
502	[[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]) when programming ES within a
503	session. Use the 5-10 minute per-muscle-group ceiling and the electrode-placement guidance
504	as baseline practical limits if ES is added to a programme, and restrict direct-over-nerve
505	placement to trained personnel.
506	
507	**When NOT to apply** — The sequencing citations (Purvin, Deniskin, Khodykin) give no dates,
508	sample sizes, or effect-size numbers in this passage, only a directional ranking of four
509	conditions (ES-then-plyometrics; plyometrics-then-ES; ES+plyometrics+heavy resistance
510	concurrent; ES+plyometrics during rest); treat this as a single-lab directional finding, not
511	a quantified prescription. The authors' own recommendation against untutored use, and the
512	legal restrictions they cite, mean this entry should not be read as a self-administration
513	guide; it summarises the book's own cautions, not a certified protocol.
514	
515	**Example** — Inference: a strength coach considering adding ES to a plyometric-heavy block
516	should schedule the ES stimulus before the plyometric work in the same session (per the
517	cited ranking), keep any single muscle group's intense ES exposure under 10 minutes, and use
518	adjacent electrode placement for a more localised, superficial target versus distant
519	placement for a deeper, more extensive contraction.
520	
521	**Related** — [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]],
522	[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]],
523	[[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]].

538	# Muscle Recruitment Stays Fairly Consistent at Moderate Loads but Shifts Toward Proximal Muscles as Resistance or Velocity Rises
539	
540	**What it is** — Two related findings on how muscle involvement changes with load and
541	velocity during repetitive barbell lifting. First, the "most stable indicator" of
542	coordinated muscular activity in repetitive lifting is the sequential involvement of the
543	same specific muscles across reps: in an experiment at 60% of 1RM, the muscles taking part
544	in the work remained the same for 82% of the time across all athletes tested; at 80% of
545	1RM, consistency was lower (showing greater individuality), but higher among qualified
546	athletes than novices, and fatigue also disrupted coordination (Pakhomov, 1967). The
547	relative contribution of participating muscles can also change during repetitive work
548	(Lazareva, 1966; Kozlov, 1966), and the number of muscle groups involved can either decrease
549	(Moikin, 1964) or increase (Averyanov, 1963) as a set progresses. Second, movements executed
550	with little effort or low velocity involve mostly the muscles of the body's distal links
551	(Tochilov, 1946; Kosilov, 1948; Vinogradov, 1951); against significant resistance or at high
552	velocity, activity characteristically shifts to the muscles of the proximal links, "which
553	tend to play a more tonic or postural role." The authors draw a direct implication from this
554	second finding: "muscle isolation under conditions of significant resistance is impossible,"
555	a point developed later in the chapter (see
556	[[claim--muscle-isolation-is-load-dependent-mostly-illusory-under-heavy-load]]). (PDF p.
557	229, printed p. 218, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training.")
558	
559	**Why it works** — No explicit mechanism is given for why recruitment consistency at 60% of
560	1RM (82%) exceeds that at 80% of 1RM, only the observation that qualified athletes show
561	greater consistency than less qualified ones at the higher load, and that fatigue disrupts
562	it further. Inference: this is consistent with the general principle that skilled athletes
563	have more stable, better-rehearsed motor patterns, which higher loads and fatigue both stress
564	more than lower loads. For the proximal/distal shift, the authors give no mechanism beyond
565	the empirical citations; Inference: this is plausibly related to proximal muscles' larger
566	cross-sectional area and postural/stabilising role becoming more necessary as the system
567	must resist larger external forces or move faster.
568	
569	**When to apply** — Use the 60%-vs-80%-of-1RM recruitment-consistency finding as a caution
570	when interpreting EMG or force-plate data collected across a set: consistency of which
571	muscles are active can itself change with load and fatigue state, independent of the
572	athlete's technique intent. Use the proximal/distal shift finding when auditing exercise
573	selection for "isolation" claims at high resistance: expect proximal, postural muscle
574	involvement to increase, not stay constant, as load or velocity rises. **Eric's baseline:**
575	this is directly relevant to interpreting force-plate strategy metrics (phase durations,
576	which segments contribute) that vary with load, per the department's driver/strategy metric
577	framework (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
578	`hd-odsf-metrics.md`).
579	
580	**When NOT to apply** — These are single-lab, era-specific findings (Pakhomov 1967;
581	Lazareva/Kozlov 1966; Moikin 1964; Averyanov 1963; Tochilov 1946; Kosilov 1948; Vinogradov
582	1951) without reported sample sizes, exercise types, or modern replication in this text; the
583	specific 82% figure applies to Pakhomov's particular protocol at 60% of 1RM, not a general
584	constant. Do not assume the direction of the number-of-muscle-groups change (increase per
585	Averyanov vs decrease per Moikin) is reconciled in the text; both are cited as findings
586	without explanation of why they differ.
587	
588	**Example** — Inference: an assistant coach comparing an athlete's EMG-active muscle groups
589	on an early, light-effort warm-up set against a heavy top set within the same exercise
590	should expect to see a proximal shift in the heavy set (more trunk/hip involvement) even if
591	technique looks visually similar, per this claim; this is a monitoring inference, not stated
592	in the source.
593	
594	**Related** — [[claim--muscle-isolation-is-load-dependent-mostly-illusory-under-heavy-load]]
595	(the chapter's own forward reference, 4.2.9, which this claim explicitly anticipates),
596	[[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]] (Ch3, a related finding
597	on how effort in one muscle group spreads to others).

# Case Study: Siff's First-Hand Account of Serge Reding's Electrostimulation Protocol

**What it is** — This passage is Siff writing in the first person about his own direct
training contact with Serge Reding, a Belgian superheavyweight weightlifter, "who had close
training contact with one of the authors (Siff) while he stayed with him in South Africa in
the early 1970s" (citing Siff, 1973). Reding's post-session electrostimulation (ES) protocol
differed from Kots's (see
[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]): 0.5 to 2 second, very
high intensity contractions with 10 to 15 second rest periods, for a total of 5 minutes per
major muscle group, with agonists and antagonists of each limb alternately stimulated in
ipsilateral and contralateral sequences. Reding always concluded sessions with a few
repetitions (1-3) of a long-duration (10-15 second), fairly intense tetanic contraction
used as a form of deep massage, followed by about 10-15 minutes of microcurrent stimulation
(less than 200 microamps) applied across the head and spinal cord with a separate
electrostimulator. Elsewhere in the section, Siff again writes in the first person: "the ES
training applied to the author by Serge Reding used a Myogen Parametric stimulator that was
designed to offer external stimulation which in no way simulated the most frequently
occurring movements of Olympic lifting," used as a form of General Physical Preparation
(GPP) rather than sport-specific stimulation; Reding stressed the importance of different
waveforms and regimes for different sport categories, "adding that the method shared by
Kots with Canadian coaches was only one of many possibilities." (PDF p. 220, printed p.
209; PDF p. 226, printed p. 215, "4.2.1.1" and "4.2.1.6 The Use of Electrostimulation in
Training.")

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why this specific dosing pattern (brief,
high-intensity contractions; alternating ipsilateral/contralateral agonist-antagonist
sequencing; a closing deep-massage-style tetanic contraction; low-current cranial-spinal
microstimulation) would produce a training effect; the passage is a descriptive account of
practice, not an experiment.

**When to apply** — Inference: use this as a documented example that elite-level ES
protocols in this era varied substantially even among people working with the same broad
technology (faradic/interferential ES devices); it is not evidence that Reding's specific
protocol outperformed Kots's, only that it existed and was applied to a top-level athlete
under Siff's direct observation.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: this is a single first-person account (n = 1, Siff
observing/administering) with no reported outcome data (no before/after strength numbers),
no control condition, and no independent replication in the text. Do not treat the specific
timings (0.5-2s contractions, 10-15s rest, 5 min per muscle group, 10-15 min microcurrent
under 200 microamps) as a validated prescription; they are a description of what one
coach-athlete pair did.

**Example** — The book's own example is this case itself: Reding's own protocol as directly
witnessed and partly administered by Siff. No further invented example is added here.

**Related** — [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]],
[[claim--ratov-functional-electrostimulation-emg-triggered-sport-specific]] (a different,
contemporaneous Soviet approach Siff also directly observed).

# Kots's 20%+ Electrostimulation Strength Claims Drew Western Interest but Were Not Replicated

**What it is** — American interest in electrostimulation (ES) as a training adjunct was
aroused in 1971, when Kots in Russia reported increases of more than 20% in muscle
strength, speed and power produced by several weeks of "electrotraining." Unable to
produce comparable results, Canadian researchers invited Kots to lecture at Concordia
University in 1977; armed with the detail that Kots used a sinusoidally modulated 2500 Hz
current source applied in a sequence of 10 seconds of contraction followed by 50 seconds of
relaxation, they again tried to duplicate the Russian claims. The authors report that "researchers
continue to disagree on increase in muscle strength" despite this, and separately note that
various track coaches reported success integrating conventional faradic ES into a
carefully periodised training programme (Francis, 1982). (PDF pp. 219-220, printed pp.
208-209, "4.2.1.1 The Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation.")

**Why it works** — The authors give no physiological mechanism for why Kots's specific
protocol (2500 Hz carrier, 10s on/50s off) would or would not replicate; the chapter's
later "Reasons for Conflicting Research" subsection (see
[[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]]) gives the general
methodological reasons ES research disagrees, without resolving the Kots case specifically.

**When to apply** — Inference: treat any single large ES strength-gain percentage (here,
"more than 20%") as a claim tied to one specific, fully-specified protocol (waveform,
frequency, duty cycle) from one lab, not a generic property of "electrostimulation" as a
category; the Canadian replication attempt failed using a different protocol until they
obtained Kots's exact parameters, and even then the authors do not report the Canadian
outcome as a confirmed success.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single historical claim and a single replication attempt,
both from the 1970s, without independent modern confirmation in this text. Do not cite "20%
plus" as an expected or typical ES strength gain; the chapter itself frames Kots's number as
contested rather than settled, and the following subsection lists nine separate
methodological reasons why ES strength research across studies disagrees.

**Example** — Inference: a strength coach considering NMES for a rehabilitating athlete
should ask what specific waveform, frequency and duty cycle any cited study used, since this
entry shows that even a direct attempt to replicate one well-specified protocol required
obtaining that protocol's exact parameters from its originator before a comparable attempt
could be made.

**Related** — [[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]],
[[case-study--reding-electrostimulation-protocol-siff-account]] (a contemporaneous but
differently-designed elite-athlete ES protocol the authors set against the Kots/Canadian
history).

# Nine Reasons Electrostimulation Strength Research Disagrees: A Checklist for Reading It

**What it is** — The authors give nine specific methodological reasons why published
electrostimulation (ES) strength-training studies contradict one another: (1) many studies
measure only isometric or isokinetic strength change and neglect power, speed, muscular
endurance, residual muscle tension, muscle growth and rate of neuromuscular recovery; (2)
much research uses injured or rehabilitating patients, untrained individuals, or trained
subjects of differing backgrounds, and strength gains are proportionately larger early in
training or in untrained subjects, with early gains driven mainly by neuromuscular
adaptation and learning rather than hypertrophy; (3) ES effectiveness depends on current
intensity and individual tolerance of discomfort, and no waveform has been found to be
universally most comfortable, with considerable inter-subject variation (Delitto & Rose,
1986; Mannheimer & Carlsson, 1979; Moreno-Aranda & Seirig, 1981); (4) effects depend on
waveform type and frequency, since slow-twitch and fast-twitch fibres have distinct
recruitment patterns and functional characteristics (Lloyd et al, 1986; Mannheimer &
Carlsson, 1979; Pette & Vrbova, 1985), and higher frequency (especially with a carrier
wave) lowers electrode-skin impedance and raises comfort; (5) electrode type, size, number,
location and gel affect delivered energy, resultant contraction force and comfort, and many
studies omit these details, "so valid comparisons largely are meaningless"; (6) most
studies use commercial stimulators that vary only a few of the many possible stimulation
parameters (frequency, waveform, pulse-width, modulation type, impulse interval, energy
delivered), so no single study has examined the full parameter space, even in the more
extensive review by Lloyd et al (1986); (7) ES effects, like plyometric training, may be
enhanced or diminished by how well it is integrated into an overall strength and
sport-specific programme (e.g. Francis, 1982); (8) many training regimes are deficiently
designed, setting ES intensity at a fixed value (or a fixed percentage of maximal voluntary
isometric/isokinetic contraction) that does not progress as the subject adapts, the same
flaw that limits fixed-load weight training; (9) the design and effects of a stimulator
depend on which physiological model of cellular communication it assumes (the
action-potential model versus subthreshold/bioelectric models), a design choice most
commercial stimulators do not make explicit (see
[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]]). (PDF pp. 220-221, printed pp.
209-210, "4.2.1.2 Reasons for Conflicting Research.")

**Why it works** — The authors' own framing: these are methodological confounds (measurement
scope, subject population, dosing, hardware specification, and underlying physiological
model), not evidence for or against ES itself; a study that controls for none of these nine
factors cannot be meaningfully compared with one that controls for a different subset.

**When to apply** — Use this as a checklist before citing any single ES strength-training
study: what outcome was measured (item 1), who were the subjects (item 2), was the current
intensity and waveform reported and justified (items 3-4, 6), were electrode details given
(item 5), was the training programme context described (item 7), and did the dosing
progress with adaptation (item 8)? A study missing several of these items should be treated
as weak evidence regardless of its stated conclusion.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this checklist evaluates methodological rigor, not
whether ES "works"; a study can satisfy all nine points and still report a negative or null
result, and the authors elsewhere report both positive and negative ES findings that passed
some of these criteria (see
[[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]]). Do not use this list
to dismiss all ES research wholesale; use it to weight individual studies.

**Example** — Inference: a marketing claim citing "a study showing 20% strength gains from
electrostimulation" should be checked against this list: was the outcome purely isometric
(item 1)? Were the subjects untrained or rehabilitating (item 2)? Was the current intensity
fixed for the whole programme (item 8)? Failing several of these checks should lower
confidence in the claim regardless of the headline number.

**Related** — [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]],
[[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]].

# Seventeen Claimed Clinical and Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation, With Their Original Citations

**What it is** — The authors catalog electrostimulation's (ES) reported applications and
effects, each with cited sources: (1) increase in muscle strength, strongest in
incapacitated, unfit or weakest subjects, with ES alone at best matching or trailing
voluntary exercise, though periodised programmes combining ES with training sometimes
increased competitive athletes' strength (Francis, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Matteson,
1984; Reding, 1973); (2) re-education of faulty muscle-action patterns, e.g. chondromalacia
patellae, tennis elbow, "frozen shoulder" (Eriksson, 1981; Godfrey et al, 1979; Johnson et
al, 1977; Nirschl & Sobel, 1981); (3) facilitation of contraction when voluntary contraction
is blocked by disuse, pain or injury, reducing tissue wasting; (4) increased muscular and
systemic endurance from prolonged sub-maximal ES, with low-frequency (under 15 Hz),
24-hour continuous stimulation shown in animal studies to shift fast-twitch fibres toward a
more aerobic, fatigue-resistant profile (Jolesz & Sreter, 1981; Pette, 1984; Pette & Vrbova,
1985; Salmons & Vrbova, 1969; Salmons & Henriksson, 1981); (5) increased speed of
contraction from long-term, higher-frequency (over 40 Hz) ES, improving reaction time and
decreasing time-to-peak-tension of fast-twitch fibres (Fleury & Lagasse, 1979; Salmons &
Vrbova, 1967, 1969); (6) increased local blood supply, with measured increases from about
20% to over 200%, greatest below roughly 30 Hz (Currier et al, 1986; Richardson, 1981;
Wakim et al, 1948; Wakim, 1953); (7) a massage-like pumping action on venous/lymphatic
return; (8) pain relief via TENS, using low-frequency (50-100 Hz) stimulation without
contraction for superficial pain, or short, high-intensity bursts (1-150 Hz) with
contraction for deeper pain; (9) reduction of protective muscle spasm and spasticity; (10)
promotion of relaxation and recuperation, attributed to central endorphin/enkephalin
release, used by Russian athletes for post-training recuperation and to aid sleep onset even
with mild thigh-only stimulation; (11) increased range of movement, used alongside PNF
mobilisation; (12) reduction of non-infectious swelling; (13) halting or slowing mild to
moderate scoliotic curvature with ES applied to specific back muscles (Axelgaard et al,
1983; Friedman et al, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Schultz et al, 1981); (14) preferential
recruitment of the largest-diameter motor axons first, the reverse of natural recruitment
order, making them a supplementary route to axons that are hard to activate under normal
training (Enoka, 1988); (15) an acute strength increase after a single session: Alon (1985),
studying 14 subjects, found one experimental ES session produced a mean 13% increase in
quadriceps strength; (16) improved metabolic economy: Ratov & Kryazhev (1986) found
electrically stimulating the quadriceps during cycling and speed skating reduced oxygen
consumption by 10-17% and extended time-to-fatigue by 15-20%, and treadmill running with ES
reduced oxygen consumption by about 10%, or by about 5% if the stimulated muscles had just
performed the work; (17) increased contractile speed of skeletal muscle via phasic-type ES.
(PDF pp. 221-224, printed pp. 210-213, "4.2.1.3 Clinical Applications of
Electrostimulation.")

**Why it works** — The authors give a distinct proposed mechanism for each effect
(catalogued above per item) rather than one unifying mechanism; several (items 4-5, 14, 17)
are tied to fibre-type recruitment and conversion, while others (6-13) are tied to blood
flow, central neurochemistry, or mechanical pumping action. Inference: no single theory in
this passage ties all seventeen together; the authors' own attempt at unification is the
separate MACS/MICS theory (see
[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]]).

**When to apply** — Use this as a reference catalog when deciding whether ES could serve a
specific, narrow purpose (e.g. swelling reduction, pain relief, post-training recuperation)
distinct from strength development, which the authors treat as ES's weakest and most
contested claimed benefit (see
[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]). Inference: for Athletic
Medicine or Applied Performance settings, items 6-13 (blood flow, pain, spasm, swelling,
recuperation, ROM) map most directly onto standard rehabilitation and recovery use cases,
while items 1-5, 14-17 (strength, endurance, speed, recruitment, metabolic economy) are the
more contested performance-training claims.

**When NOT to apply** — Each item rests on citations from roughly 1948-1988, mostly single
studies or small samples (e.g. Alon's 13% figure is from 14 subjects, one session); none are
independently re-validated within this ingest. Item 4's fibre-type conversion evidence is
from animal (cross-innervation, continuous 24-hour stimulation) studies, not directly
transferable to standard clinical ES dosing. Do not treat this list as equally strong
evidence across all seventeen items; some (blood flow, pain relief, swelling) have broader
citation support here than others (scoliosis, acute strength).

**Example** — Inference: a post-training recovery application (item 10, low-current
stimulation to aid relaxation and sleep onset) is a narrower, better-supported use case than
citing this same list to justify ES as a primary strength-training tool (item 1, contested
above); a practitioner should not conflate the two when deciding whether to add ES to a
program.

**Related** — [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]],
[[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]],
[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]].
