# Power Output Peaks and Declines With Load in a Barbell Jump, but Falls Steadily in a Leg-Press, Because of Elastic Energy

**What it is** — As barbell load increases, work increases, but power output is not
unidirectional: for a jump with a barbell on the shoulders, power output initially
increases, then, once barbell weight exceeds about 66% of maximum, it begins to decrease
(Chikvadze, 1961). Maximum power output for this jump is achieved with weights of 30-40% of
1RM, and maximal reactivity coefficient at 30-33% of 1RM. Verified against the page image
(Fig 4.2, printed p. 217): as load rises from 14% to 86% of max strength, maximal force
(Fmax) and movement time both rise, while power and the reactivity coefficient (R) show a
non-monotonic pattern across the load range rather than rising or falling steadily
throughout. The authors attribute the rise in power and reactivity coefficient with
increasing movement time to "additional elastic energy accumulated in the muscles by
absorbing the kinetic energy of the body and apparatus during the amortisation phase." A
contrasting experiment removes that elastic-energy source: seated leg extensions from a
110-degree initial knee angle, lifting 20/40/60/80% of maximum concentrically with no
countermovement or amortisation phase. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.3, printed p.
217): here, maximal force and movement time again increase with resistance, "analogous to
jumps with a barbell," but power output decreases progressively across the whole load range
instead of peaking mid-range, "because the extra elastic energy is lacking in this case."
(PDF pp. 216-217, printed pp. 216-217, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training," Figs 4.2-4.3.)

**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is the presence or absence of an
amortisation (countermovement/stretch-shortening) phase that stores and releases elastic
energy: the jump-with-barbell condition includes this phase, so at moderate loads the added
elastic-energy return can boost power and reactivity even as load rises, up to the point
(about 66% of max) where added weight overwhelms that benefit; the seated leg-extension
condition has no comparable amortisation phase, so power falls steadily as soon as
resistance climbs, since only added resistance (not stored elastic energy) is changing.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution when generalising a load-power relationship from
one exercise type to another: a countermovement or stretch-shortening exercise (jump,
countermovement press) can show power peaking at a specific submaximal load band (here,
30-40% of 1RM for maximal power, 30-33% for maximal reactivity), while a purely concentric,
no-amortisation exercise (seated leg extension here) shows power declining steadily as load
rises, with no such peak. Inference: this is consistent with why "optimal power load"
testing protocols (e.g. jump squats across a load spectrum) find a load band that maximizes
power, while purely concentric single-joint machine exercises typically do not show the same
peak.

**When NOT to apply** — This is single-lab, era-specific data (Chikvadze, 1961; Siff &
Verkhoshansky, 1999 figure redraws) on unspecified subjects; the specific percentages
(66% threshold, 30-40% for max power, 30-33% for max reactivity) should be treated as
illustrative for this particular jump-with-barbell protocol, not as universal constants for
all jumping or pressing exercises. Do not assume every loaded jump variation shows peak
power at exactly 30-40% of 1RM; load-power curves are known to vary by exercise and by
population in the modern literature, which this passage does not address.

**Example** — Inference: a coach programming loaded jump squats for maximal power output
should expect the power curve to rise then fall across the load spectrum (consistent with
Fig 4.2's pattern), and should not extrapolate that same rise-then-fall shape to a
non-countermovement exercise like a seated leg press or leg extension machine, where this
entry's Fig 4.3 data show power declining steadily as load increases instead.

**Related** — [[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]],
[[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (a related but distinct
reactivity-coefficient formulation from a different protocol, Ch3.2.1).

# Inertial (Flywheel) and Elastic Resistance: Different Force Profiles From Free Weights, Each With Its Own Limitation

**What it is** — The authors note that specialised equipment for training against a load's
inertia (rather than its weight) is rarely used, despite the concept warranting more serious
attention. Two solutions are given: applying force against a horizontal wheel or a
suspended, pendulum-like load, or spinning a heavy flywheel ergometer with the arms or legs
(Fig 4.4, elbow-flexion flywheel device, Verkhoshansky 1977). A flywheel device's moment of
inertia can be varied to change the speed-of-contraction demand, and it can be used several
ways: accelerating against high inertia, using the wheel's momentum to compel a certain
movement cadence, or opposing the wheel's angular momentum via eccentric muscle action to
decelerate it, with these methods combinable in short or mixed bursts. Elastic bands are
treated as a separate special case: resistance follows Hooke's Law (F = kx, where k is the
spring constant and x is extension), so elastic force starts at zero and rises with range of
movement; the authors state plainly that "elastic materials should not be used for
developing starting-strength in ballistic movements or for developing explosive-strength,"
because those qualities need force available from the very start of the movement, which
elastics cannot supply. For strength-endurance over a selected range, however, an elastic
band's length and elasticity can be chosen so its resistance changes minimally over the
working range, a method used by swimmers to develop pulling strength-endurance (Fig 4.5,
Verkhoshansky 1977). Resistance at "sticking points" can be reduced by moving toward the
band's attachment point, or increased by moving away from it; resistance can also be varied
across the full range by accelerating free weights through a decreasing-resistance portion
of the lift (so-called Compensatory Acceleration Training, see
[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]]) or by using dedicated variable-resistance
machines. (PDF pp. 219-220, printed pp. 219-220, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training,"
Figs 4.4-4.5.)

**Why it works** — For flywheel/inertial devices, the mechanism is that resistance is
determined by the load's inertia (F = ma) rather than its weight (F = m(g+a)), so the
athlete can train speed of contraction against a resistance that does not exist at rest, only
once acceleration is applied, unlike a gravity-loaded free weight. For elastic bands, the
mechanism is Hooke's Law itself: resistance is proportional to extension, so it is
inherently near-zero at the start of the range and maximal at the end, the opposite loading
curve from what ballistic and explosive-strength work typically needs (high force available
immediately).

**When to apply** — Use flywheel/inertial devices when the training goal is speed of
muscular contraction against inertia specifically (per
[[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]]), varying moment of inertia to
adjust the demand, and consider eccentric-deceleration use of the same device for eccentric
overload. Use elastic bands specifically for strength-endurance work over a selected range
(the authors' cited example: swimmers' pulling strength-endurance), choosing band length and
elasticity to minimise resistance variation across that range, and use position along the
band (closer to or farther from the attachment) to manage sticking-point loading.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use elastic-band resistance alone for developing
starting-strength or explosive-strength in ballistic movements; the authors state this
directly, since Hooke's Law resistance is lowest exactly when ballistic/explosive movements
most need force to be available. The flywheel and pendulum devices described are
purpose-built or improvised apparatus (a 1992 University of the Witwatersrand student
biomechanics project supplied the plyometric bench-press device shown nearby, Fig 4.6, a
related but separate kinetic-energy device); the authors give no standardised commercial
specification for the flywheel or pendulum devices described here.

**Example** — Inference: a swim coach building pulling strength-endurance with resistance
bands, per the authors' own cited example, should select a band whose resistance changes
little across the stroke's working range, rather than a stiffer band whose resistance would
spike sharply near full extension; a sprint or jump coach chasing starting-strength or
explosive-strength should not substitute elastic-band resistance for free weights or
inertial-device training for that specific quality.

**Related** — [[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]],
[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]].

# Two Ways Resistance Exercises Develop Force: Against a Load's Weight, or Against Its Inertia

**What it is** — The authors distinguish resistance exercises by two different bases: first,
by whether the working force is developed after preliminary muscular tension already equal
to the apparatus's weight (e.g. the starting position of a squat or squat jump, where the
legs and torso have already developed tension equal to the barbell's weight before the
dynamic effort begins), or whether force is developed essentially from zero without
appreciable preliminary tension (e.g. the snatch or clean-and-jerk, where the working force
accelerating the bar starts from near zero). The first group does not appreciably influence
the excitation-tension processes in the muscle and, depending on the weight used, chiefly
develops either muscular strength or speed of contraction, but not the speed of switching
from rest to active state; the second group has "simultaneous potential for developing
dynamic strength, speed of movement and especially starting strength." Second, and
separately, the authors classify exercises by which physical quantity the force is directed
against: force against the weight of a load (F = m(g+a), determined by the load's mass and
its acceleration against gravity, e.g. lifting a barbell), or force against the inertia of a
load (F = ma, dependent only on the load's inertial force at a given acceleration, e.g.
throwing, sprinting out of blocks, punching, where force acts roughly perpendicular to
gravity). In the first (overcoming weight) case, muscular force first equals the load's
weight (developed under virtually isometric conditions), then exceeds it as motion begins,
producing "a large gradient of acceleration-strength." In the second (overcoming inertia)
case, if friction and air resistance are excluded, movement begins with insignificant
propulsive force, and further force changes depend entirely on the speed of muscular
contraction, i.e. the muscle's simultaneous production of maximal strength and maximal speed
of contraction. Consequently, resisting a load's weight primarily stimulates the strength
component, while resisting a load's inertia primarily stimulates the speed of muscular
contraction. (PDF pp. 218-219, printed pp. 218-219, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength
Training.")

**Why it works** — The mechanism is straightforward Newtonian mechanics: F = m(g+a) versus F
= ma describe two different physical situations a muscle can be asked to produce force
against, and the authors' point is that a muscle's neuromuscular demand differs between
starting from a preloaded isometric-like state (weight-bearing) and starting from
essentially unloaded rest and having to generate speed against only inertia. The "large
gradient of acceleration-strength" in the weight-bearing case follows from force already
being non-zero (equal to the load's weight) at the instant motion begins, unlike the
inertia-only case, which starts from near-zero force.

**When to apply** — Use the preliminary-tension distinction (loaded-start vs
from-zero-start) to classify which exercises best target starting strength specifically:
per this framework, exercises that begin from essentially zero muscular tension (snatch,
clean-and-jerk, and by extension sprint starts, punches, throws) uniquely combine dynamic
strength, movement speed and starting-strength development, while loaded-start exercises
(squat, squat jump) do not train the speed of switching from rest to active state in the
same way. Use the weight-versus-inertia distinction to separate exercises meant to build
raw strength capacity (heavy squats, deadlifts) from those meant to build speed of
contraction against a light or unloaded resistance (medicine-ball throws, sprint
acceleration drills, punching).

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this is a biomechanical classification of the demand an
exercise places on the neuromuscular system, not a training-volume or periodization
prescription; the authors do not state how much of each type of exercise to program, only
that the two types target different qualities. Do not assume every "explosive" exercise
falls cleanly into one category; many sport movements (e.g. a jump shot, a football block)
mix a loaded start with subsequent inertia-dominated acceleration, and this framework
addresses the two idealized cases, not every blend.

**Example** — Inference: a back squat (loaded start, force against weight) and a standing
broad jump with no external load (unloaded start, force against inertia) place different
demands on the same lower-body musculature per this framework: the squat's preliminary
tension already equals the bar's weight before the concentric drive begins, while the broad
jump must generate all of its propulsive force from a near-zero starting tension, making
starting strength and speed of contraction the dominant qualities rather than absolute force
capacity against a heavy external weight.

**Related** — [[claim--power-output-peaks-then-declines-with-load-jump-vs-leg-press]],
[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]] (Ch1, a related point that free-weight
resistance already varies with acceleration per Newton's second law).

# The Optimal Depth-Jump Drop Height Is 0.75-1.15 Metres: Maximal Power at the Low End, Maximal Force at the High End

**What it is** — Verified against the page image (Fig 4.7, printed p. 221): comparing three
vertical-jump conditions by force (in bodyweights) against time, (1) jumping from rest from
a low squat produced the lowest and latest force peak and a jump height of 0.67 m; (2) the
usual jump with a dip/amortisation phase produced a higher, earlier force peak and 0.74 m;
(3) a jump after a depth-jump from 0.4 m produced the highest and earliest force peak and
0.80 m (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Extending this to depth jumps from a range of drop heights
(Fig 4.10, printed p. 223): maximal force (Fmax) increases with drop height up to 1.15
metres, then diminishes sharply; movement time changes little at first, then increases
sharply at greater drop heights; maximum power output and maximum reactivity are both
achieved at a drop height of approximately 0.75 metres. The authors state the optimal range
of depth jumping for stimulating muscular activity is therefore 0.75-1.15 metres: "at the
lower end of this range the muscles are working at maximal power and at the upper end they
are working at maximal dynamic force." This finding underlies the training recommendations
for advanced jumpers (Verkhoshansky 1963, 1964, 1966), though the authors recommend erring
toward considerably lower drop heights for anyone unaccustomed to this training and strictly
limiting volume of this "shock" training. Beyond 1.15 metres, ground-contact (support) time
increases quickly, primarily because the eccentric-to-concentric switching phase lengthens,
while maximum dynamic force and contraction speed at take-off stabilise and stop increasing.
The take-off is described as two distinct phases: amortisation (kinetic energy absorbed,
characterised by progressively deeper knee flexion) and thrust proper (characterised by a
fairly constant speed of muscle contraction). (PDF pp. 222-223, printed pp. 221-223,
"4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes," Figs 4.7, 4.9, 4.10.)

**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is again elastic-energy storage during
amortisation and its release in the thrust phase (see
[[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]]); at greater drop
heights, force capacity is used mainly for braking (absorbing more kinetic energy),
explaining why force keeps rising up to 1.15 m while power and reactivity peak earlier (at
0.75 m), once the added braking demand from a higher drop starts to lengthen the
amortisation phase and slow the eccentric-to-concentric switch.

**When to apply** — Use 0.75 m as a drop height when the training goal is maximal power and
reactivity, and up to about 1.15 m when the goal is maximal dynamic force, per this specific
protocol; for athletes unaccustomed to depth-jump training, start considerably lower than
this range and strictly limit training volume, per the authors' own caution. This gives a
citable historical anchor for programming depth-jump height, distinct from (and using a
different, variable-height protocol than) the fixed 0.4 m depth-jump reactivity test already
in this library (see [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]).

**When NOT to apply** — This is single-lab, era-specific data (Verkhoshansky, 1963-1977) on
an unspecified population (the authors do not state training age, sport, or sample size for
the drop-height range experiment); the specific numbers (0.75 m, 1.15 m) should not be
applied to every athlete without accounting for training age, technical competency and
bodymass, which the authors themselves flag by recommending lower heights for the
unaccustomed athlete. Do not conflate this protocol's variable drop-height range with the
separate, fixed-0.4-m depth-jump reactivity test already documented in this library (see
Related); they are different experiments answering different questions (optimal training
drop height here, versus a reactive-ability measurement protocol there).

**Example** — The book's own example is the Fig 4.7 and Fig 4.10 data described above; no
further invented example is added here.

fixed-0.4 m depth-jump protocol measuring reactive ability rather than optimal training drop
height),
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].

# Heavier Falling Loads Reduce How High They Get Thrown, but Falling From Higher Reduces It Less: The Kinetic-Energy Throw Experiment

**What it is** — A laboratory stand measured the height a subject could throw a load
upward after it had first fallen from a set height (0.5 to 3.0 metres), with load
expressed as a fraction of the subject's maximum isometric strength (Po): 3.3%, 6.6%,
9.9% and 13.3% of Po (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Verified against the page image (Fig 4.8a,
printed p. 222): as fall height (h1) increases from 0 to 3 metres, throw height (h2)
rises for every load, but the lighter loads (3.3% Po) reach a substantially greater throw
height at every fall height than the heavier loads (13.3% Po), and the heaviest load's
curve flattens and slightly declines at the greatest fall heights rather than continuing to
rise. The authors summarise: "an increase in kinetic energy caused by an increase in the
mass of the load decreases the height to which a load is thrown, but an increase in the
distance through which a load falls increases the height to which it is thrown." A similar
pattern appears for reactive ability (Fig 4.8b, reactivity coefficient plotted against the
falling load's kinetic energy in joules): verified against the page image, each load curve
(3.3%, 6.6%, 10%, 13.3% Po) is an inverted-U shape rising to a peak reactivity coefficient
then declining as kinetic energy increases further, with the peak's position and height
differing by load (the lightest, 3.3% Po, load reaches the highest peak reactivity
coefficient, around 7, at a moderate kinetic energy). The authors conclude "it is not
beneficial to increase kinetic energy by use of heavier loads," and that a better means of
increasing thrust height is needed. (PDF pp. 221-223, printed pp. 221-222, "4.2.3 Kinetic
Energy and Strength Processes," Fig 4.8.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no separate mechanism beyond the shared elastic-energy
logic already stated for this section (see
[[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]]): a heavier load
carries more kinetic energy at a given fall height (KE = mgh scales with mass), but that
extra energy appears to exceed what the muscle can productively absorb and return within a
short amortisation phase, so throw height and reactivity fall off rather than continuing to
rise with load. Inference: this is consistent with an optimal-loading phenomenon where
elastic-energy return and voluntary concentric contribution both have a productive range,
beyond which added mass mainly adds braking demand rather than usable stored energy.

**When to apply** — Use this as evidence against assuming "more kinetic energy equals more
training stimulus" when programming falling-load or catch-and-thrust exercises (e.g. weighted
plyometric throws, loaded catch-and-press devices): per this experiment, increasing the drop
height is a more productive way to raise thrust/throw height than increasing the load,
within the tested range (0.5-3.0 m fall heights, 3.3-13.3% of isometric strength as load).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab (Verkhoshansky, 1977) experimental stand using a
narrow load range expressed relative to isometric strength (Po), not a standard external
load; the specific percentages and the shape of the reactivity-coefficient curves should not
be assumed to transfer directly to other exercises, populations, or load types (e.g. a
barbell drop-catch versus this stand's specific apparatus) without direct testing. The
authors do not report the subject population or sample size for this experiment.

**Example** — The book's own example is this experimental stand and its Fig 4.8 data; no
further invented example is added here.

**Related** — [[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]],
[[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]],

reactivity-coefficient protocol using a fixed 0.4 m depth jump with externally added mass
rather than this section's variable fall-height, variable-load-as-%-of-Po stand).

# Stimulating Muscle by Absorbing a Fall's Kinetic Energy: The Mechanics and Five Claimed Advantages Over Weighted Resistance

**What it is** — When a training device such as a barbell falls from a height and the
athlete's task is to actively stop it, then quickly thrust it upward (Fig 4.6, a purpose-built
plyometric bench-press device from a 1992 University of the Witwatersrand student
biomechanics project), the total muscular working force developed by eccentric amortisation
followed by active concentric work can be calculated as F = m(V1^2/2S1 + g) + m(V2^2/2S2 +
g), where V1 and V2 are the barbell's velocity at displacements S1 and S2 (derived from V^2 =
u^2 + 2as). Much of the falling apparatus's kinetic energy converts, during the amortisation
phase, into elastic energy used in the subsequent concentric work; excluding losses such as
heat and viscous damping as a first approximation, this elastic energy equals the kinetic
energy at the end of the fall (KE = mgh, where h is the fall height). Muscular force at the
eccentric-to-concentric switch is greater for a shorter amortisation phase and shorter
braking time, provided the goal is to thrust the apparatus at maximum speed immediately
after stopping it. The authors state the external mechanical stimulus here is "not so much
the weight (and its force of inertia) as the energy accumulated after its free-fall,"
distinguishing this from ordinary weighted resistance (see
[[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]]). Drawing on the vertical-jump
data in Fig 4.7 (see
[[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]), the authors list five claimed
advantages of this stimulation method: (1) it develops maximal dynamic force very rapidly;
(2) the magnitude of that maximum is significantly larger than other methods produce; (3) a
large maximal force is achieved without additional resistance; (4) the eccentric-to-concentric
switch happens far more rapidly than with other methods; (5) the elastic energy accumulated
without additional resistance produces greater power and faster contraction in the thrust
phase, inferred from the greater jump height reached. (PDF pp. 220-222, printed pp. 220-221,
"4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes," Fig 4.6.)

**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is elastic-energy storage and release during
the amortisation phase (the same mechanism underlying the shock method, see
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]), combined with the mechanical
stimulation of proprioceptors at the instant of an abrupt stretch when a falling body is
stopped (citing Ramsey 1944; Hill 1955; Tweit et al 1963), which the authors say "creates the
conditions for developing starting strength and explosiveness of muscular action" that "no
heavy resistance exercise can imitate," because stimulating muscular activity with
significant extra resistance slows the eccentric-to-concentric transition.

**When to apply** — Use this framework's five advantages as the stated rationale for
programming falling-body/kinetic-energy stimulation (depth jumps, plyometric catches) rather
than purely weighted resistance when the specific goal is starting strength and explosive
strength, per the authors' own claim that these qualities are acquired slowly through
ordinary resistance training because they require unusually stressful, high-intensity
conditions that most popular resistance exercises do not reliably provide even though they
also start force development from rest.

**When NOT to apply** — The force formula (F = m(V1^2/2S1 + g) + m(V2^2/2S2 + g)) and the KE
= mgh approximation explicitly exclude heat generation and viscous damping "as a first
approximation," so treat it as a simplified model, not an exact measurement of muscular
force in vivo. The five advantages are presented as the authors' own summary claims from the
Fig 4.7 jump data (see
[[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]), not as independently
replicated findings across other kinetic-energy-stimulation exercises; do not extend them
uncritically to every falling-load exercise without checking that exercise's own data.

**Example** — The book's own example is the depth-jump/plyometric-bench-press apparatus
described above (Fig 4.6); see
[[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]] for the specific numeric
findings this framework's advantages are drawn from.

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (Ch1, the shock-method
terminology and elastic-energy mechanism this framework builds on),
[[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]],
[[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]],
[[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]].

# Four Ways to Stimulate Working Muscular Tension, and How They Map to the Rest of the Chapter

**What it is** — External muscular force is a product of voluntary effort, but voluntary
effort alone has limits; the authors classify how "stimulation of working force" is
supplied from outside that voluntary effort into four basic types: (1) muscular tension
produced by voluntary effort against external resistance, where the moving load's
resistance "accelerates and regulates the effector impulses to the muscles"; (2)
stimulation by the kinetic energy of a falling object or the body, where "the effort is
primarily reflexive"; (3) stimulation caused primarily by voluntary effort under conditions
where additional external mechanical stimulation is absent or limited; and (4) stimulation
of muscle "elicited or intensified involuntarily by means of external electrical current."
The authors group the first two as dynamic work and the third as isometric work; for the
first, increased stimulation comes from increasing the velocity of the preliminary fall of
the body or load; for the third, from "mobilising the athlete's voluntary resources."
Voluntary effort plays an important role in the first case, but is "insignificant" in the
second (the falling-body case), where the braking/amortisation mechanism produces a
protective reflex response faster than a voluntary sequence of actions can. This forms the
basis of plyometric training (see [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]).
This four-way classification sets up the rest of the chapter's structure: type (4) is
covered next as 4.2.1 Electrostimulation, type (1) as 4.2.2 Resistance and Strength
Training, type (2) as 4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes, and type (3) as 4.2.4
Isometric Training. (PDF p. 218, printed p. 207, "4.2 Different Means of Strength
Development.")

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reason: afferent impulses elicited by mechanical
stimulation inform the central nervous system about the strength of the external
influence evoking muscular tension, and "the greater the intensity of the external
stimulus, the greater the muscle effector discharge, and the larger the external work
produced." Inference: this is a general afferent-feedback framing rather than a
mechanism specific to any one of the four types; the chapter's later sections give more
detailed, type-specific mechanisms (e.g. elastic energy storage for the falling-body case,
gradual overload for the resistance case).

**When to apply** — Use this as an organizing checklist when auditing a program's strength
means: does a given exercise stimulate tension primarily through external resistance,
through absorbed kinetic energy (a fall or catch), through sustained voluntary effort with
little external aid (isometric), or through externally applied electrical current? Mixing
means from more than one category (e.g. resistance plus electrostimulation) is a distinct
programming decision from staying within one category, and the chapter's later sections
(4.2.1 Electrostimulation, "Sports Functional Electrostimulation") discuss combining
categories explicitly.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this is the book's own convenience classification for
organizing chapter 4.2, not a claim that these four mechanisms are mutually exclusive
within a single exercise (a depth jump followed by a jump, for example, combines kinetic-
energy stimulation with subsequent voluntary resistance work). Do not treat the four-way
split as a measurement protocol; it carries no associated testing method here.

**Example** — Inference: a coach comparing a paused back squat (voluntary effort against
external resistance, type 1), a depth jump (kinetic energy of a fall, type 2), a wall sit
(sustained voluntary isometric effort, type 3), and a quadriceps NMES session (external
electrical current, type 4) is comparing four different stimulation mechanisms for the same
target muscle group, each covered by a different subsection of this chapter. This example
is not in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (Ch1, the falling-body
mechanism this framework's type 2 builds on); [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]
(Ch1, the mechanical regimes -concentric, eccentric, isometric- this framework's types map
onto at the muscle-action level, a distinct but adjacent classification).

2	                                                               SUPERTRAINING
3	
4	     One more feature should be noted. I f the given means do not elicit an adequate training effect, then increase
5	mworkcapacity becomes more a factor o f specialised exercise than training volume and then only i f it is executed
6	bytraining at or near personal maximum levels. It should be pointed out that the execution o f specialised
7	exercises in training at near maximal intensity (as advocated by Bulgarian experts) should be regarded as an
8	advanced strategy, a method which cannot be acknowledged as being universally appropriate. This would imply
9	not only rejecting the principles o f the rational structuring of training based on research into training methods, but
10	alsoa return to the original concepts from which these began.
11	
12	     Thus, the problem o f establishing scientifically the means o f sport training is far from being solved and the
13	current tendency to increase the volume o f the training load should not detract from its significance and turn the
14	attention of specialists away from its in-depth study.
15	
16	     If a logical sequence is to be recommended as a practical solution to the problem o f improving the
17	effectiveness o f special strength training methods, then it should be laid down as follows:
18	
19	      1. Regime -- 2. Means --  3. Methods --  4. System --  5. Volume
20	
21	From this scheme it follows that the means o f special strength training should be selected on the basis of
22	quantitative descriptions o f the motor specificity o f the given sport and thereby provide an adequate regime of
23	work for the body. The basic criterion for this is a guarantee o f a definite training effect for the given level o f
24	special fitness.
25	
26	    The next step is to determine a suitable method o f using the means based not only on the specific m otor
27	regimes of the given sport, but also on factors such as one's level o f fitness and the tasks o f the current stage o f
28	training. Of great potential for perfecting the methods o f special strength training, is the principle o f systematic
29	application o fmeans to produce the necessary cumulative training effect.
30	
31	    Finally, attaining the necessary level o f special strength training depends on the volume o f the special work,
32	theoptimal magnitude o f which should be determined by the stage and current tasks o f the athlete's preparation,
33	thecompetition calendar and the intensity o f the load.
34	
35	    This scheme emphasizes that, to rely on any one parameter o f the load for achieving any given potential is
36	appropriate only after the potential o f the previous parameter has been completely exploited. For example, it is
37	unwise to increase training volume without having fully elicited the maximum training effect o f the individual
38	strength training means at a particular intensity. This requires dedication and persistence from the specialists,
39	because it requires in-depth investigative effo rt Since increasing the training volume is easier than finding a really
40	effective means o f special preparation, such a course tends to be a much simpler choice.
41	
42	4.2 Different M eans o f S t r e n g th D ev e lo p m e n t
43	
44	Theexternal force generated by muscles is a result o f voluntary effort. However, under normal everyday
45	conditions, muscular tension produced by voluntary effort has certain limitations. To increase the external
46	muscular force it is necessary to stimulate them from the outside, for example, by means o f mechanical
47	stimulation. Afferent impulses elicited by mechanical stimulation inform the central nervous system about the
48	strength of the external influence evoking the muscular tension. The greater the intensity o f the external stimulus,
49	thegreater the muscle effector discharge, and the larger the external work produced.
50	
51	    Thus, afferent signals to the neuromuscular system play an important role in determining the qualitative and
52	quantitative characteristics o f muscular strength. Therefore, the stimulation o f muscular tension for the
53	development o f strength is o f great significance. So, in all cases the magnitude o f working muscular tension is
54	determined by voluntary effort and external mechanical action. The stimulation o f working force can be divided
55	 intothe following basic types:
56	
57	   � Stimulation when muscular tension is produced by voluntary effort against external resistance, and the
58	      resistance o f the moving load accelerates and regulates the effector impulses to the muscles
59	
60	   � Stimulation by the kinetic energy o f a falling object or the body, when the effort is primarily reflexive
61	
62	   � Stimulation caused prim arily by voluntary effort, under conditions where additional external mechanical
63	      stimulation is absent or limited
64	
65	   � Stimulation o f muscle elicited or intensified involuntarily by means o f external electrical current.
66	
67	                                                                  207
68	 ######## PDF idx 219 (viewer 220)
69	                                                                   SUPERTRAINING
70	
71	The first tw o cases are associated with dynamic work and the third with isometric work. An increase in
72	stimulation is realised in the first case by increasing the velocity of the preliminary fall o f the body or load, and by
73	mobilising the athlete's voluntary resources in the third. It should also be pointed out that voluntary effort plays
74	an im portant role in the m agnitude o f the effector response o f the m uscles in the first instance, whereas its
75	influence in the second is insignificant.
76	
77	     The mechanism chiefly responsible for the braking or amortisation work o f the muscles causes a protective
78	effector response more rapidly than a voluntary sequence of actions. Therefore, such a reflex stimulus is able to
79	provoke an extraordinary mobilisation o f the neuromuscular apparatus, which is impossible where there is reliance
80	on voluntary effort alone. This mechanism forms the foundation o f plyometric training (5.2.4).
81	
82	4.2.1 E le c tr o stim u la tio n
83	
84	As has already been stated, there is always an ongoing search for novel, highly effective means o f special strength
85	training. For example, Russian studies have established that clcctrostimulation o f muscle furnishes an adequate
86	training stimulus for effective development o f muscular strength (Kots, 1971; Kots & Khvilon, 1971; Khvilon,
87	1974). Electrostim ulation can be effective for certain purposes in the preparation o f highly qualified athletes
88	(mainly in speed-strength sports) and there are a number o f advantages associated with this method o f developing
89	strength, in particular the reduction o f joint loading. It can occupy a specific place in the yearly training cycle, be
90	used in combination with other methods o f developing muscular strength and be applied chiefly in the preparation
91	of highly qualified athletes.
92	
93	     Ratov has found that functional electrical stimulation (FENS) can be particularly useful in improving sporting
94	performance. His techniques, developed decades ago from his PhD programme on the interrelation between
95	electrical stimulation and electromyography, has used EMG signals from agonist and antagonist muscles to act as
96	triggers or control mechanisms for electrical stimulation o f musclcs directly involved in producing functional
97	m ovem ents in sport. In his laboratory at the State Central Institute for Sports Science in M oscow he has
98	successfully implemented these neuromuscular stimulation methods in training athletes such as fencers, boxers,
99	rowers, shotputtcrs and weightlifters.
100	
101	      However, it is inappropriate to consider the training applications o f electrostimulation in detail here because
102	its methodological fundamentals have still not been determined, especially as it should be applied preferably under
103	suitable conditions by qualified personnel. The next section summarises the effects and applications of
104	electrostimulation as a form of supplementary sports preparation.
105	
106	4.2.1.1 The Physiological Effects of Electrostim ulation
107	
108	The concept o f elcctrostim ulation is not new, and for years has been used by physical therapists in clinical
109	applications such as muscle rehabilitation, relief o f muscular spasm, reduction of swelling and pain control. Its
110	possible value in sports training is still considered controversial. In strength conditioning, the applications of
111	electrostimulation fall into the following broad categories:
112	
113	   � Imposition o f local physical stress to provoke supercompensation
114	   � Local restoration after exercise or injury
115	   � General central nervous and endocrine restoration after exercise or injury
116	   � Neuromuscular stimulation for pain control or movement patterning
117	
118	Electrostimulation usually involves feeding the muscles low current electrical impulses via moistened electrode
119	pads placed firmly on the skin. The effectiveness, comfort and depth o f excitation depends on factors such as
120	pulse shape, frequency, duration, intensity and modulation pattern. The resulting number o f possible stimulation
121	combinations immediately emphasizes how difficult it is to determine the optimum balance o f variables and
122	compare the results o f different researchers.
123	
124	     The typical clinical machine supplies pulsating direct (galvanic) and/or alternating (faradic) current in the form
125	o f brief pulses. The frequency o f faradic current is most commonly chosen in the range o f about 50-100 Hz, while
126	pulse duration (width) ranges from about 100 microseconds to several hundred milliseconds. This brevity of pulse
127	duration is important to minimise skin irritation and tissue damage. However, the duration at any particular
128	intensity o f faradic stimulation should not be too brief Although they may be suitable for decreasing pain, pulses
129	that are too brief will supply insufficient energy to cause full, tetanic muscle contraction.
130	
131	                                                                     208
132	 ######## PDF idx 220 (viewer 221)
133	                                                                SUPERTRAINING
134	
135	     Machines are designed to apply alternating currents directly at a preset or selected frequency (conventional
136	faradism), or in the form o f low frequency currents superimposed on a medium frequency (2000 to 5000 Hz)
137	earner wave. A variation o f the latter method, using two pairs o f electrodes each supplying medium frequency
138	waves carrying low frequency waves differing slightly in frequency, forms the basis o f what is called interferential
139	stimulation. A major advantage o f using a higher frequency carrier wave is that impedance between the electrodes
140	andskin is lowered, enhancing comfort and effectiveness.
141	
142	     American interest in electrostim uiation as a training adjunct was aroused in 1971, when Kots in Russia
143	reported increases o f more than 20% in muscle strength, speed and power produced by several weeks of
144	dectrotraining. Unable to produce comparable results, the Canadians invited him to lecture at Concordia
145	University in 1977. Armed with the new information that Kots em ployed a sinusoidally modulated 2500 Hz
146	cunent source applied in a sequence o f 10 seconds o f contraction followed by 50 seconds o f relaxation, they again
147	triedto duplicate Russian claims.
148	
149	    It is noteworthy that this procedure differed significantly from that o f top Belgian superheavy weightlifter.
150	Serge Reding, who had close training contact with one o f the authors (Siff) while he stayed with him In South
151	Africa in the early 1970s. After training sessions he used 0.5 to 2 second, very high intensity contractions with
152	10to 15 second rest periods, for a total o f 5 minutes per major muscic group, with agonists and antagonists o f
153	each limb alternately stimulated in ipsilateral and contralateral sequences (Siff, 1973). Reding always concluded
154	his sessions with a few repetitions (1-3) o f a long duration (10-15 seconds) fairly intense tetanic contraction to
155	serve as a type o f deep massage, followed by about 10-15 minutes o f microcurrent stim ulation (less than 200
156	microamps) applied across the head and spinal cord with another electrostimulator.
157	
158	      Despite the subsequent success reported by various track coaches in integrating conventional faradic
159	electrostimulation into a carefully periodised training programme (Francis, 1982), researchers continue to disagree
160	onincrease in muscle strength.
161	
162	4.2.1.2 R eason s for C o n flictin g R esearch
163	
164	There are several main reasons for the contradictory research findings:
165	
166	1. Many studies focus largely on isometric or isokinetic strength changes, which complicates research
167	comparisons. Such research often neglects possible effects o f other vital factors such as power, speed, muscular
168	endurance, residual muscic tension, muscle growth and rate o f neuromuscular recovery.
169	
170	2. Much of the research examines injured patients in the process o f rehabilitation, untrained individuals, or trained
171	subjects from differing fitness and training backgrounds. It is well known that an increase in strength is
172	proportionately greater in the early stages o f a training programme or among untrained subjects. Moreover,
173	increases in strength for novices during the first few weeks o f training mainly are due to neuromuscular adaptation
174	andlearning, rather than muscle hypertrophy.
175	
176	3. The effectiveness o f electrostim uiation is determined by the intensity o f the current used and individual
177	tolerance of discomfort caused by stimulation. In addition, no specific waveform has been found to be universally
178	most comfortable. There also can be considerable variation among subjects in their response to different
179	waveforms and stimulation impedances (Delitto & Rose, 1986; Mannheimcr & Carlsson, 1979; Moreno-Aranda
180	&Seirig, 1981).
181	
182	4. The effects o f electrostim uiation depend on the types and frequency o f waveforms used, particularly since
183	 there is a distinct difference in the recruitment patterns and functional characteristics o f slow-twitch and fast-
184	 twitch muscle fibres (Lloyd ct al, 1986; M annheimer & Carlsson, 1979; Pette & Vrbova, 1985). Moreover, the
185	 higher the frequency, particularly if a carrier wave is used, the lower the impedance between electrodes and skin,
186	 andthe greater the degree o f comfort.
187	
188	 5. The type, size, number and location o f electrodes, as well as the electrode gel, affect the amount o f electrical
189	 energy transmitted to the muscles, the resultant force o f contraction and patient comfort. M any studies do not
190	 discuss these details, and therefore, valid comparisons largely are meaningless.
191	
192	 6. Most studies have used com m ercial electrostim ulators which arc able to vary only a few o f all the possible
193	 stimulation parameters. Some o f the more extensive studies have varied several o f these parameters, as
194	 summarised in the thorough review by Lloyd et al (1986). However, because o f the enormous number o f
195	
196	                                                                   209
197	 ######## PDF idx 221 (viewer 222)
198	                                                                   SUPERTRAINING
199	
200	stimulation combinations theoretically possible, no single extensive study has been able to examine the effects of
201	varying all the stimulation parameters. This includes frequency, waveform, pulse-width, type o f modulation
202	(Frequency Modulation, Amplitude Modulation or pulse-width modulation), impulse interval and electrical
203	energy delivered.
204	
205	7. The effects o f electrostim ulation, like plyometric training, may be enhanced by optimal integration into an
206	overall strength and sport specific training programme (e.g. Francis, 1982)
207	
208	8. Many o f the training regimes have been deficiently designed. Usually, the electrostimulator is selected according
209	to the maximum tolerated by subjects, or to a certain percentage o f a maximal voluntary isometric or isokinetic
210	contraction as measured on isokinetic or other dynamometers. It should be noted that adaptation to any stimulus
211	occurs, and subjects can withstand greater intensities o f electric current from the start to end o f any session, and
212	from week to week.
213	
214	     Similarly, studies examining the combined effects o f electrostimulation and normal strength training often
215	prescribe weight training with a fixed number o f sets and loads at a fixed percentage o f single repetition maximum,
216	despite the fact that the latter maximum gradually increases. The accompanying electrical stimulation also is set at
217	a fixed value, which fails to consider that the basic principle o f strength and power enhancement is gradual
218	overload. Such a training regime in normal weight training is known to be highly limited in improving physical
219	performance. It would be surprising if it were any different with electrostimulation training.
220	
221	9. The design and effects o f the electrostimulator depend on the choice o f physiological model. Most stimulators
222	are designed on the basis o f the action-potential model o f nerve cell discharge, which considers that cellular
223	communication in the body is mediated by bursts o f electrical discharge transmitted along nerve axons. The cell is
224	assumed to be W (discharging electricity) or 'off (resting), depending on whether the build-up o f electrical charge
225	in the cell is large enough to exceed a certain threshold, rendering the cell membrane temporarily more permeable to
226	certain chemical ions. Intermediate subthreshold states arc presumed unimportant, although they are central to an
227	understanding o f the EEG (brain waves) and other electrical potentials o f the central nervous system (Siff, 1981).
228	
229	       Sim ilarly, the numerous glial cells which surround all nerve cells are assum ed to play little more than a
230	nutritional or supportive role for the nerves, despite the fact that they display a steady or quasi-steady electric
231	field (Galambos, 1961; Siff, 1981). Some scientists believe that glial cell potentials may have a profound effect on
232	nerve cells by modulating their activity similar to semiconductors such as transistors in electronic circuits (Becker.
233	1974; Galambos, 1961). In addition, the DC injury potentials measurable on the skin surface after tissue damage
234	are not associated with the action potential system (Becker, 1982).
235	
236	       Moreover, little is known about electrical fields at the subcellular level. The sensitivity o f the body to
237	external electric, magnetic and electromagnetic fields cannot satisfactorily be explained in terms of action
238	potentials, which are not directly affected by these fields (Becker, 1965; Cope, 1974). The classical theories also
239	do not explain the mechanisms whereby electric and other fields stimulate processes such as the repair of
240	fractures, the healing o f wounds and reduction o f thrombosis.
241	
242	     On discovering evidence for semiconduction and the possible existence o f superconductivity at room
243	temperature in biological systems, scientists now have postulated that tissue healing, pain mechanisms, cell
244	growth and disease processes may involve biological semiconduction and superconductivity (Becker, 1965; Cope,
245	1971; Cope, 1974). In addition, Nordenstrom claims to have shown the presence o f closed electric circuits in the
246	body, whereby ionic flow concerned with growth and regulatory processes takes place via blood vessels and
247	through or along the capillaries (Nordenstrom, 1983).

249	     All faradic, medium frequency and interferential stimulators (including sports-oriented machines) are designed
250	on the action-potential model for cell operation, which, therefore, do not permit applications relying on the other
251	types o f models described above. Such applications involve cell growth, tissue repair and general recuperation, all
252	o f which are essential features o f physical conditioning. In recent years a few innovative micro-current machines
253	based on these models have been applied clinically with significant success in neuromuscular rehabilitation (Chee
254	& Walton, 1986; Matteson, 1984; Matteson & Eberhardt, 185; Meyer & Nebrensky, 1983; Noto & Grant, 1985).

412	4.2.1.4 Further R esearch Findings
413	
414	Recent research and clinical experience have revealed that electric currents as much as 1000 times smaller than that
415	ofall the traditional physical therapy modalities can be far more successful than the latter in achieving many o f
416	the benefits outlined in the previous section.
417	
418	     Currents as low as 10 microamps (millionths o f an amp) pulsating at between 0.1 to 400Hz are too weak to
419	cause muscle contraction, block pain signals or cause local heating, yet their effectiveness and safety is often
420	superior in many applications to that o f faradism, interfercntialism and conventional TENS (M atteson &
421	Eberhardt, 1985).
422	
423	    The steps to satisfactorily modify the existing paradigm for ES may be sought in the research findings quoted
424	earlier in the section: 'Reasons for conflicting research'. There, it was learned that cellular and subcellular
425	processes not involving cell discharge, propagated electrical impulses, or muscle contraction, appear to be
426	involved with cellular growth and repair.
427	
428	      Some studies have produced findings which offer partial answers to the questions posed by
429	microstimulation. For instance, work by Becker and others suggests that small, steady or slowly varying currents
430	cancause sub-threshold modulation o f the electric fields across nerve and glial cells, thereby directly regulating cell
431	growth and communication (Becker, 1974; Becker & Marino, 1982). In this respect, some o f Becker's applications
432	included the acceleration o f wound healing, partial regeneration o f amphibian and rat limbs, and induction of
433	narcosis with transcranial currents. Nordenstrom maintains that these electric currents can stimulate the flow of
434	ions along the blood vessels and through the cell membranes which constitute the body's closed electric circuits
435	postulated by his theory (Nordenstrom, 1983).
436	
437	     Pilla (1974) has paid particular attention to electrochemical information transfer across cell membranes. The
438	 model in this case hypothesizes that the m olecular structure o f the cell mem brane reflects its current genetic
439	activity. Here, the function o f a cell at any instant is determined by feedback between DNA in the cell nucleus and
440	
441	amacromolecule inducer liberated from the membrane by means o f a protein (enzym e) regulator derived from
442	
443	 messenger RNA activity within the cell. The activity o f these membrane-bound proteins is strongly modulated by
444	 changes in the concentration o f divalent ions (such as calcium Ca"^) absorbed on the membrane. ES may elicit
445	 these ionic changes and thereby modify cell function.
446	
447	     It has been shown that ES at 5Hz stim ulates synthesis o f DNA in chick cartilage cells and rat bone by as
448	 much as 27%, but not in chick skin fibroblasts or rat spleen lymphocytes (Rodan et al, 1978). Not only does the
449	 effect of ES appear to be tissue-specific, but the increase in DNA synthesis occurs 4-6 hours after 15 minutes o f
450	 ES. The process o f membrane depolarisation carried by sodium ions seems to be followed by an increase in
451	 intracellular Ca4^ concentration, thereby triggering DNA synthesis in cells susceptible to the particular stimulus.
452	 Further work by Pilla (1981) has confirmed the existence o f cellular 'windows' which open most effectively to
453	 certain frequencies, pulse widths and pulse amplitudes. To attune the ES signal to these parameters, monitoring o f
454	 tissue impedances is preferable, a system employed by so-called 'Intelligent TENS' devices.
455	
456	     In addition, Cheng et al (1982) have shown that stim ulation with currents from 50-1000 m icroamps can
457	 increase tissue ATP concentrations in rats by 300-500%, and enhances amino acid transport through the cell
458	 membrane and consequent protein synthesis by as much as 40% . Interestingly, the same study reported that
459	 increasing the current above only one milliamp was sufficient to depress tissue ATP and protein synthesis - and
460	 traditional ES usually applies currents exceeding 20 milliamps, at which stage this depression being nearly 50%.

466	4 .2 .1 .5 An Integrated Theory o f E lectrostim ulation
467	
468	Therefore, it appears as if macroelectric cellular stimulation (MACS - currents exceeding one milliamp) acts asa
469	physiological stressor, which in the short term causes the typical alarm response described by Selye (1975). This
470	is supported by the work o f Eriksson et al (1 9 8 1), who found that the acutc effects o f traditional ES are similar to
471	those found for intense voluntary exercisc. Furthermore, Gambkc ct al (1985) have found in animal studies that
472	long-term MACS causes some musclc fibres to degenerate and be replaced by newly formed fibres from satellite
473	cell proliferation. This fibre necrosis occurs a few days after application o f ES and seems to affect mainly the FT
474	fibres. The fact that the various muscle fibres do not transform at the same time may be due to different
475	thresholds o f each fibre to the stimulus that elicits the transformation. Possibly, the earlier changes might induce
476	subsequent ones.
477	
478	       Thus, if Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome model (see 1.16) is applied to M ACS-type stimulation, the
479	body w ould have to draw on its superficial adaptation energy stores and adapt to the ES-im posed stress by
480	increasing strength or endurance, or by initiating transformation o f musclc fibre types. If the ES is too intense, too
481	prolonged or inappropriately used to augment a weight training programme, adaptation might not occur or it might
482	increase the proportion o f slow twitch fibres and thereby reduce strength. This could explain some o f the negative
483	research findings discussed earlier.
484	
485	       Furthermore, excessively demanding MACS conceivably might cause the body to draw on its deep
486	adaptation energy and lead to permanent tissue dam age. Consequently, any athlete who may derive definite
487	performance benefits from MACS should not assume that increased dosage will lead to ftirther improvement. The
488	contrary may well prove to be true.
489	
490	       Microelectric cellular stimulation (MICS - currents below one milliamp), on the other hand, would not act as
491	a stressor. Instead, the evidence implies that it elicits biochemical changes associated with enhanced adaptation,
492	growth and repair. Since MICS appears to operate more on the basis o f resonant attunement o f the stimulus to
493	cellular and subcellular processes, the specific therapeutic effects are determined by how efficiently the
494	stimulation parameters match the electrical characteristic o f the different cells, in particular, their impedance at dif
495	ferent frequencies. MICS may be applied in several ways to facilitate restoration:
496	
497	   � locally over specific soft tissues
498	   � transcranially via electrodes on the earlobes or on sites on the surface o f the skull
499	   � at acupuncture points on the body, hands or ears.
500	
501	It is generally entirely safe to apply MICS anywhere on the body, because the current and energy transmitted is
502	too low to produce any thermal or electrolytic effects on vital tissues. Under no circumstances should MACS be
503	applied across the brain, as it can cause serious harm. It is generally not advisable to apply any form o f ES to
504	epileptics, pregnant women, cardiac patients or persons with heart pacemakers.

506	4 .2 .1 .6 The Use o f E lectrostim ulation in Training
507	
508	The summary o f successful applications o f ES in numerous situations which are relevant to all athletes makes it
509	unfortunate that its value has been assessed largely in terms o f its direct and often contradictory effects on
510	isometric or isokinetic strength. Enhanced recuperation, improved endurance, diminished residual muscle tension,
511	pain relief, efficient massage, modification o f muscle fibre type, increase in mobility, increased speed of musclc
512	contraction and reduction o f certain musculoskeletal abnormalities together supply an impressive variety of pos
513	sible aids to any training programme. Coupled with this is the observation that some ES procedures integrated
514	into carefully periodised training schedules may significantly increase strength, muscular endurance and power.
515	
516	The Integrated Use o f E lectrostim ulation
517	
518	Electrostimulation can provide a valuable additional means o f restoration and is generally ofgreater importance
519	than as a means o f stressing the muscles. This type o f restoration (Siff & Yessis, 1992) may be applied locally to
520	specific muscle groups, other soft tissues or joints, or generally across the central nervous system (transcranially,
521	on specific acupuncture points or between the brain and the lumbar spine), using very low current devices at low
522	frequencies (characteristically between 0.5-8 Hz).
523	
524	      Several researchers (Purvin, Dcniskin, Khodykin) studied the integration o f ES into other regimes o f training.
525	They found that the use o f ES first, followed by plyometrics produces a greater training effect than the reverse

552	Little or no mention is made in the West o f the application o f FES (Functional Electrostim uiation) in sports
553	training. In the West, this term or its equivalent FENS (Functional Electroneural Stimulation) invariably applies
554	to the use o f electrostim uiation to contract the m uscles o f spinally disabled patients who cannot voluntarily
555	activate their muscles and offer some degree o f externally controlled movement. In Russia and other Eastern
556	European countries the terms can also apply to the application o f electrostimuiation to able-bodied athletes during
557	natural sporting movements to intensify muscle tension at the most appropriate phases o f these movements. The
558	innovative Professor Igor Ratov o f the State Central Institute o f Sports Science in Moscow, has done considerable
559	research in this field with able-bodied and disabled subjects and stresses that this type o f functional stimulation is
560	far more consistently successful than the passive methods attributed to Kots by his Western supporters.
561	
562	     Work that I witnessed in his laboratory involved the use o f concurrent EMG recordings to phase the FES
563	correctly into specific sporting movements, most specifically to avoid producing spurious muscle tension or
564	uncoordinated movement. Eventually, athletes leam to contract their muscles synchronously with the externally
565	applied electrical field and thereby produce greater strength, power and speed. This method is som etim es called
566	active electrostimuiation, since the ES is applied to active musclcs rather than to relaxed muscles (passive
567	electrostimuiation), which is the method most commonly used in physical therapy.

569	     The use o f highly specific methods like sports FES should not lead us to exclude the possible importance o f
570	general methods o f ES which intentionally avoid offering any form o f functional training. In this respect, the ES
571	training applied to the author by Serge Reding used a Myogen Parametric stim ulator that was designed to offer
572	external stimulation which in no way simulated the most frequently occurring movements o f Olympic lifting. In
573	other words, ES may also be used as a form o f GPP (General Physical Preparation). The Reding machine applied
574	 brief intense pulses alternately in a flip-flop fashion to opposite sides of the body, though not to paired agonists
575	 and antagonists. The intensity o f the ES was carefully periodised into the entire training programme alongside
576	 other key methods o f strength training and training sessions were always terminated with brief, deep ES muscle
577	 massage and restorative microstimulation across the brain and along the length o f the spinal cord. Reding stressed
578	 the importance o f different waveforms and regimes o f FES for different categories of sport, adding that the
579	 method shared by Kots with Canadian coaches was only one o f many possibilities.

603	Concluding Remarks
604	
605	The untutored reader is not encouraged to use ES, since it requires considerable theoretical and practical training
606	for its safe and effective application. Those who experiment casually with such devices in training generally note
607	sporadic or short-term progress and discontinue their use after just a few months. Unless applied by experts in

614	4.2.2 R esistance and Strength Training
615	
616	In principle, the heavier the weight which muscles lift, the greater the tension they develop. The latter is achieved
617	by the effective stimulation and recruitment into the work o f a large proportion o f the involved musclcs. Strength
618	development through the use o f resistance activity was demonstrated around 500 BC by the legendary Milo of
619	Crotona. According to legend, he increased his strength enormously by lifting a young bull daily onto his
620	shoulders. As the bull grew in mass, so did Milo's strength.
621	
622	       In our own era Milo's approach is exemplified by the DeLorme method o f progressive resistance exercise
623	(DeLorme, 1945; DeLorme & Watkins, 1948, 1951). Essentially, this method consists o f developing strength
624	through repetitively lifting a weight which is gradually increased in the workout, as well from workout to
625	workout, as strength increases.
626	
627	       However, when the display o f great force was required, the imposition o f resistance was a natural means of
628	training, but where speed o f movement plays a decisive role, resistance was used initially with great care. At the
629	same time, some researchers noted that strength training makes it possible to improve results in speed type
630	exercises (Dupperon, 1926; Lubimov, 1927; Curie, 1937; Markov, 1938, Ozolin, 1939; Chui, 1950; Gullwer,
631	1955; Pennybaker, 1961). However, a long period o f experimental and practical verification was required before
632	this hypothesis gained acceptance. However, it is correct only relative to the amount o f weight, the coordination
633	pattern o f the movement, the tempo and the number o f repetitions.
634	
635	     When resistance is used for stimulating m uscular tension, it is necessary to consider the fact that strength
636	may be displayed in resistance exercises in the form o f maximal tension or maximal speed o f muscle contraction.
637	One can then refer to strength exercises in which force is displayed primarily by increasing the amount of weight,
638	and speed-strength exercises in which the display o f force is associated with increasing the speed o f movement
639	(Farfel, 1940). In the first case, one tries to work with the largest resistance possible and in the second with a
640	resistance whose optimal magnitude is determined by the required speed o f movement.
641	
642	      It should be pointed out that the work regim es o f strength with primarily slow movements and speed-
643	strength exercises (using inherently fast movements) are essentially different with respect to the physiological
644	mechanisms and the manner in which energy resources are used. Execution o f explosive movements invariably
645	requires a high level o f excitation of the basic neural processes. In the case o f slow movements, the basic role of
646	the nervous system is to produce sufficient excitation and maintain it for a relatively long period (Federov, 1957).
647	
648	      It is useful to examine more closely the dynamics o f movements with maximal effort in terms of the
649	magnitude o f the resistance displaced and the regime o f muscular work. The amount o f work obviously increases
650	as the load raised by a weightlifter is increased. However, the changes in the power output o f the w ork arc not
651	unidirectional. Initially, power output increases, but after the weight o f the barbell exceeds 66% o f maximum, it
652	begins to decrease (Chikvadze, 1961). A similar result is observed in the jump with a barbell on the shoulders (Fig
653	4.2). Maximal dynamic force increases as the weight o f the apparatus increases during the rapid increase in the
654	movement time, mainly during the active thrust phase. Maximum power output is achieved with weights of 30-
655	40% o f the IRM and a maximal coefficient o f reactivity at 30-33% o f the 1RM.
656
