# Review: Supertraining 4.2 intro and 4.2.1-4.2.3 (round 1, Opus)

Reviewer: Claude Opus, independent round-1 reviewer, 2026-09-27. Read-only on the entries and sources.
Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`. Locators below are 0-based PDF idx = printed + 11 (viewer = idx + 1). I read the text layer for idx 218-235 and opened every figure as a page image: Fig 4.2 and 4.3 (idx 228 / p.217), Fig 4.6 (idx 231 / p.220), Fig 4.7 (idx 232 / p.221), Fig 4.8a and b (idx 233 / p.222), Fig 4.9 and 4.10 (idx 234 / p.223), with zoomed crops of 4.2, 4.3, 4.7, 4.8, 4.9 and 4.10.
Scope: the 15 files in `_scope_supertraining_ch4-2a.txt`.

## Batch-wide problems (each one is also listed in the rows)

A. **Wrong PDF locators in six entries.** The power, inertial, two-force, depth-jump, thrown-load and kinetic-framework entries give "PDF pp." equal to the printed page. The PDF page is printed + 11. Correct values are given in each row.
B. **Figures described as "verified against the page image" but misread.** Fig 4.7, Fig 4.8a and Fig 4.8b are described wrongly (see the depth-jump and thrown-load rows). The 09-27 lesson applies: a figure is "verified" only when the description matches the image.
C. **Internal contradictions in the source that were not recorded.** Reding's agonist/antagonist sequencing (p.209 vs p.215), Kots/ES "established" (p.208) vs "continue to disagree" (p.209), Fmax past 1.15 m "diminishes sharply" vs "stabilise" (p.222), Fig 4.3 caption "leg-press" vs text "seated leg extensions", and Fig 4.8a vs its text summary.
D. **Unlabelled writer's mechanisms and prescriptions.** Several "Why it works" and "When to apply" sections, listed per row.
E. **Safety claims.** The book's explicit ES safety rules on idx 225 / p.214 appear in no entry. These are: MICS "generally entirely safe" anywhere; "Under no circumstances should MACS be applied across the brain"; "not advisable to apply any form of ES to epileptics, pregnant women, cardiac patients or persons with heart pacemakers". The MICS safety claim ("cannot produce overtraining or injury", p.215) is quoted, but no entry says that the book gives no safety data for it.

## Entry table

| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs source, with page) | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| case-study--reding-electrostimulation-protocol-siff-account.md | FIX | (1) Voice. Entry: "This passage is Siff writing in the first person". The p.209 passage is third person: "close training contact with one of the authors (Siff) while he stayed with him" (idx 220 / p.209). Only p.215 is self-referential ("applied to the author by Serge Reding", idx 226 / p.215). (2) Role reversed. Entry: "as directly witnessed and partly administered by Siff" (Example) and "Siff observing/administering" (When NOT). The book says Reding applied ES *to* Siff: "the ES training applied to the author by Serge Reding" (idx 226 / p.215). The protocol on p.209 is what Reding himself "used" after his own sessions. (3) Contradiction not recorded. p.209: "agonists and antagonists of each limb alternately stimulated in ipsilateral and contralateral sequences (Siff, 1973)". p.215: "The Reding machine applied brief intense pulses alternately in a flip-flop fashion to opposite sides of the body, though not to paired agonists and antagonists." (4) Missing from p.215: "The intensity of the ES was carefully periodised into the entire training programme", and the closing was ES massage plus microstimulation "across the brain and along the length of the spinal cord". Entry says "regimes for different sport categories"; the book says "regimes of FES for different categories of sport". (5) "Why it works" opens "No mechanism is given" but does not say by whom. | (1) Replace the first sentence with: "The authors describe (p.209, third person) Serge Reding, 'who had close training contact with one of the authors (Siff)'. On p.215 Siff writes of 'the ES training applied to the author by Serge Reding'." (2) Replace "directly witnessed and partly administered by Siff" and "Siff observing/administering" with "received by Siff as the subject (p.215) and described from Reding's own practice (p.209)". (3) Add: "The book describes the pattern two ways. p.209: agonists and antagonists of each limb alternately stimulated, ipsilateral and contralateral. p.215: pulses alternately to opposite sides of the body, 'though not to paired agonists and antagonists'. Both are recorded; the book does not reconcile them." (4) Add the periodisation sentence (p.215) and change the quote to "regimes of FES". (5) Change to "The authors give no mechanism." Confidence `untested` is correct. |
| claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated.md | FIX | (1) "Not replicated" is the writer's word, not the book's. The book says: "Unable to produce comparable results, the Canadians invited him ... they again tried to duplicate Russian claims" and "researchers continue to disagree on increase in muscle strength" (idx 220 / p.209). It does not report the result of the second attempt. The title and the "When to apply" line "the Canadian replication attempt failed using a different protocol until they obtained Kots's exact parameters" add a claim the page does not make: nothing on the page says the first Canadian attempt used a different protocol. (2) The contradiction that makes this `contested` is omitted. idx 219 / p.208: "Russian studies have established that electrostimulation of muscle furnishes an adequate training stimulus for effective development of muscular strength (Kots, 1971; Kots & Khvilon, 1971; Khvilon, 1974)". p.211 (idx 222) lists Kots & Chwilon 1971 among ES "appears to increase the strength of competitive athletes in some instances". (3) "American interest" (book) became "Western interest" in the title, and "the Canadians" became "Canadian researchers". Minor. ## Missing ideas (covered pages, no entry)

1. **ES safety rules and contraindications** (idx 225 / p.214). "Under no circumstances should MACS be applied across the brain, as it can cause serious harm." This belongs in the safety heuristic, attributed to the authors (see batch item E).
2. **ES as restoration more than stressor** (idx 225 / p.214). ES "is generally of greater importance [for restoration] than as a means of stressing the muscles", using very-low-current devices at 0.5-8 Hz locally, transcranially or at acupuncture points (Siff & Yessis 1992). The counterweight (idx 227 / p.216) is that routine accelerated restoration "can impair the natural ability of the body to recuperate and adapt". Contrast: vault `dupuy-2018` (ES did not reduce DOMS or fatigue).
3. **Resistance for speed is mainly for novices** (idx 231 / p.220). Increasing movement speed through resistance exercise "is primarily for novice athletes ... Speed-strength against significant resistance is useful only "in certain types of muscular work, at a reasonable volume, at specific stages of training". Check for overlap with the vault `framework--strength-speed-continuum-five-zones` before writing.
4. **Loaded depth jumps and the independent training role of the amortisation phase** (idx 233-234 / p.222-223, Fig 4.9). Adding 10-40 kg to a depth jump lowers rebound height, force and RC and lengthens contact time. Reflexive tension during amortisation "enhances the ability of the muscles to switch quickly to the active state", and experience says it is not detrimental, "although further research is required". Plyometrics was "originally called the 'shock method'", with a corroborating citation list and a closing note that more work is needed (p.223). Check against the existing `framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology`.
5. **Strength vs speed-strength regimes differ physiologically** (idx 227 / p.216). Strength exercises use "the largest resistance possible", and speed-strength exercises use a resistance "whose optimal magnitude is determined by the required speed of movement" (Farfel 1940). Explosive movements need high neural excitation, while slow movements need excitation that is sustained (Federov 1957). The section also opens with the DeLorme progressive-resistance lineage.

- "In the first case by increasing the velocity of the preliminary fall" (p.208), probably meaning the second case.
- Fig 4.8 loads: text "9.9%", figure "10% Po". The thrown-load entry records both; good.

## Overall verdict

**GO AFTER FIXES.** 0 GO, 15 FIX, 0 NO-GO. No entry reverses the book's conclusion. The fixes that must be applied before promotion:

1. Correct the PDF locators in the power, inertial, two-force, depth-jump, thrown-load and kinetic-framework entries (printed + 11), and widen the four-mechanisms and Ratov locators to include idx 219 / p.208.
2. Rewrite the Fig 4.7 (depth-jump), Fig 4.8a and Fig 4.8b (thrown-load) descriptions from the images, and retitle the thrown-load entry.
3. Move the Chikvadze 66% threshold from the barbell jump to the weightlifting lift (power entry).
4. Kots: drop "not replicated" as the book's claim (label it Inference or cite an external source after reading it), add the p.208 "established" statement, and remove the invented "different protocol" detail.
5. Reding: fix the voice (third person on p.209), Siff's role (he received the ES), and record the agonist/antagonist contradiction.
6. MACS/MICS: label the mainstream-status verdicts "Inference:", correct the direction of the p.210 quote, and attribute the MICS safety claims with a note that no safety data are given.
7. Safety heuristic: add the p.214 contraindications and the MACS-across-the-brain rule, delete "Russian", and label the added mechanisms.
8. Clinical effects: fix the item 16 order and the "distinct mechanism for each" claim; flag item 14 (Gregory & Bickel 2005) and item 10 (Dupuy 2018).
9. Record every internal contradiction listed above.
10. Label the remaining unlabelled writer's mechanisms and prescriptions: nine-reasons "Why"/"When", recruitment Eric's-baseline relevance, two-force "by extension" and the broad-jump example, depth-jump braking mechanism, inertial "eccentric overload".

Reciprocal-link suggestions: power entry to and from vault `claim--maximal-power-output-load-differs-lab-vs-competition-lift`; Kots to staging `claim--strength-detraining-and-retention-timelines`; clinical effects and the safety heuristic to `research-papers/dupuy-2018-...`; Ratov to the clinical-effects entry (item 16).

## Missing ideas (covered pages, no entry)

1. **ES safety rules and contraindications** (idx 225 / p.214). "Under no circumstances should MACS be applied across the brain, as it can cause serious harm." No form of ES is advisable for epileptics, pregnant women, cardiac patients or pacemaker users. MICS is "generally entirely safe" anywhere. This belongs in the safety heuristic, attributed to the authors (see batch item E).
2. **ES as restoration more than stressor** (idx 225 / p.214). ES "is generally of greater importance [for restoration] than as a means of stressing the muscles", using very-low-current devices at 0.5-8 Hz locally, transcranially or at acupuncture points (Siff & Yessis 1992). The counterweight (idx 227 / p.216) is that routine accelerated restoration "can impair the natural ability of the body to recuperate and adapt". Contrast: vault `dupuy-2018` (ES did not reduce DOMS or fatigue).
3. **Resistance for speed is mainly for novices** (idx 231 / p.220). Increasing movement speed through resistance exercise "is primarily for novice athletes ... Initially a positive influence, it becomes negative". Exercises with weights are "not necessarily adequate for developing speed of movement ... especially for highly qualified athletes". Speed-strength against significant resistance is useful only "in certain types of muscular work, at a reasonable volume, at specific stages of training". Check for overlap with the vault `framework--strength-speed-continuum-five-zones` before writing.
4. **Loaded depth jumps and the independent training role of the amortisation phase** (idx 233-234 / p.222-223, Fig 4.9). Adding 10-40 kg to a depth jump lowers rebound height, force and RC and lengthens contact time. Reflexive tension during amortisation "enhances the ability of the muscles to switch quickly to the active state", and experience says it is not detrimental, "although further research is required". Plyometrics was "originally called the 'shock method'", with a corroborating citation list and a closing note that more work is needed (p.223). Check against the existing `framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology`.
5. **Strength vs speed-strength regimes differ physiologically** (idx 227 / p.216). Strength exercises use "the largest resistance possible", and speed-strength exercises use a resistance "whose optimal magnitude is determined by the required speed of movement" (Farfel 1940). Explosive movements need high neural excitation, while slow movements need excitation that is sustained (Federov 1957). The section also opens with the DeLorme progressive-resistance lineage.

## Unclear or contradictory spots in the source (record, do not resolve)

- Reding's stimulation pattern: agonist/antagonist alternation (p.209) vs "not to paired agonists and antagonists" (p.215).
- ES as a strength stimulus: "established" by Russian studies (p.208) vs "researchers continue to disagree" (p.209).
- Fig 4.3: caption "leg-press" vs text "seated leg extensions" (p.217).
- Past 1.15 m depth jumps: Fmax "diminishes sharply" vs "stabilise and do not increase any further" (p.222); the figure shows the fall.
- Fig 4.8a vs its summary sentence (p.222); x-axis starts at 0 while the text says 0.5-3.0 m.
- "In the first case by increasing the velocity of the preliminary fall" (p.208), probably meaning the second case.
- Fig 4.8 loads: text "9.9%", figure "10% Po". The thrown-load entry records both; good.

I reviewed all 15 entries against the pages and every figure image. The result is 0 GO, 15 FIX, 0 NO-GO; overall verdict: GO AFTER FIXES.

No entry reverses the book's conclusion, so none is NO-GO. But every entry needs at least one fix before promotion. The review is at C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\review_supertraining_ch4-2a_opus.md.

**Main problems:**
- **Wrong page numbers in six entries.** The power, inertial, two-force, depth-jump, thrown-load and kinetic-energy entries give the PDF page as equal to the printed page. It should be printed + 11. The four-mechanisms and Ratov entries also need to include PDF 219 / p.208.
- **Figures misread under "verified against the page image":**
  - Fig 4.7: curves 1 and 2 peak at about the same force. Curve 1 peaks early (about 0.08 s); curve 2 dips below bodyweight, then peaks late (about 0.5 s). The entry calls curve 1 "lowest and latest".
  - Fig 4.8a: three of the four loads peak and then fall before 3 m. The entry says throw height "rises for every load".
  - Fig 4.8b: the per-load curves mostly rise. The downward arcs are lines joining equal drop heights. The entry calls each load curve an inverted U.
- **A number on the wrong exercise.** Chikvadze's 66% threshold is for a weightlifter's lift, not the barbell jump. The jump peaks at 30-40% for power and 30-33% for reactivity (p.216).
- **Kots:** "Not replicated" is the writer's claim, not the book's. The book says the Canadians were "unable to produce comparable results", tried again, and that "researchers continue to disagree" (p.209). The entry leaves out p.208, where the authors say Russian studies "have established" that electrostimulation (ES) works as a strength stimulus. It also invents a claim that the first Canadian attempt used a different protocol. The 10 s on / 50 s off figures match the page, and no entry uses "10/50/10".
- **Reding:** The p.209 passage is in the third person. p.215 shows Siff *received* the ES from Reding; the entry says he "administered" it. The book also contradicts itself: p.209 says agonists and antagonists were stimulated alternately, p.215 says "not to paired agonists and antagonists". The entry does not record this.
- **MACS/MICS theory:** It keeps the defensible stress-response thread apart from the fringe claims (Becker, Nordenstrom, Pilla) and does not endorse them. Still:
  - Its "speculative... not mainstream" verdicts are the writer's opinion and need an "Inference:" label.
  - It uses a p.210 quote backwards: the authors were arguing *for* their alternative models there, not hedging them.
  - It repeats the book's claim that MICS "cannot produce overtraining or injury" without noting that the book gives no safety data for it.
- **Safety:** No entry carries the book's safety rules on p.214. These are: never apply high-current (MACS) ES across the brain, and no ES for epileptics, pregnant women, cardiac patients or pacemaker users. The safety heuristic also calls the sequencing researchers "Russian", which the book does not say, and adds mechanisms the page does not give.
- **Clinical-effects entry:**
  - Item 16 has the order reversed: the book says ES came shortly *before* the work.
  - It wrongly claims the book gives a mechanism for every effect.
  - It should flag two outside sources. Gregory & Bickel 2005 disputes the reverse-recruitment claim; I cited it from memory, so the fixer must read it first. The vault's Dupuy 2018 found ES did not reduce muscle soreness or fatigue.
- **Other contradictions in the book, not recorded:**
  - The Fig 4.3 caption says "leg-press" but the text says seated leg extensions.
  - Past 1.15 m, one paragraph says force "diminishes sharply" and the next says it "stabilises". The image shows the drop.
  - The book says higher drops raise throw height, but Fig 4.8a shows that only for the lightest load.
- **Unlabelled writer's judgments** also appear in the nine-reasons, recruitment, two-force, depth-jump and inertial entries. In the recruitment entry, a relevance claim is labelled as Eric's view when it is the writer's. In the two-force entry, the broad-jump example does not fit the book's own definition of force against inertia.

**Missing ideas** (listed in the report):
- the p.214 safety rules;
- the authors' view that ES matters more for restoration than as a training stress;
- resistance work for speed being mainly for novices (p.220);
- loaded depth jumps (Fig 4.9) and the separate training role of the landing phase;
- the physiological difference between strength and speed-strength training.

For an outside source on Kots's results not being replicated, Ward & Shkuratova 2002 (Phys Ther, PMID 12350217) exists. Its text was blocked, so I did not confirm what it says.
